name: Linear equations
teach:
When an equation has one unknown that appears only to the first power, collect the unknown terms on one side and the constants on the other, then divide by the coefficient. Distribute any bracket before you start, and undo addition and subtraction before multiplication and division. In general, for $a\ne 0$:
$$ax+b=c \;\Longrightarrow\; ax=c-b \;\Longrightarrow\; x=\frac{c-b}{a}$$

The core intuition here is that an equation stays true if you do the same thing to both sides. So you can peel operations off the unknown one at a time until it stands alone.

*Example:* Solve $5x-4=2(x+7)$.
$$5x-4=2x+14 \;\Longrightarrow\; 3x=18 \;\Longrightarrow\; x=6$$

*Trap:* Changing only one side, or distributing a minus sign over just the first term of a bracket. Write $-(a+b)=-a-b$.

*Check:* Put the answer back into the original equation and confirm both sides match. Here the left side is $26$ and the right side is $26$.

name: Systems of equations
teach:
When two linear equations share the same two unknowns, you want the pair of values that satisfies both, which is the point where the two lines cross. Scale an equation if needed so that one variable has opposite coefficients, add the equations, and solve for the remaining unknown. Then substitute back to find the other one. Substitution works equally well, so use whichever is shorter.
$$\begin{cases}a_1x+b_1y=c_1\\ a_2x+b_2y=c_2\end{cases}$$

The core intuition here is that adding equal quantities to equal quantities keeps an equation true. Choosing the sum so that one unknown cancels leaves one equation in one unknown.

*Example:* Solve $3x+2y=13$ and $5x-2y=11$. Adding removes $y$.
$$8x=24 \;\Longrightarrow\; x=3,\qquad 3(3)+2y=13 \;\Longrightarrow\; y=2$$

*Trap:* Reading $0=5$ as an answer. It means no solution, since the lines are parallel. A result of $0=0$ means infinitely many solutions.

*Check:* Substitute the pair into the equation you did not use for the back-substitution.

name: Quadratic solving
teach:
When an equation has the form $ax^2+bx+c=0$, or reduces to it after you move every term to one side, try to factor first. Otherwise use the quadratic formula, where $b^2-4ac$ is the discriminant. A positive discriminant gives two real roots, zero gives one, and a negative value gives none.
$$x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$$

The core intuition here is that a product is zero only when a factor is zero, so factoring gives the roots at once. When nothing factors, the formula still solves every case, because it comes from completing the square.

*Example:* Solve $2x^2-3x-5=0$, where $a=2$, $b=-3$ and $c=-5$.
$$x=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{9+40}}{4}=\frac{3\pm7}{4}\;\Longrightarrow\; x=\frac52 \text{ or } x=-1$$

*Trap:* Students often slip on the sign of $-b$, or forget that $2a$ divides the whole numerator and not just the root.

*Check:* The roots sum to $-\frac{b}{a}$, which is $\frac32$ here.

name: Factoring patterns
teach:
When a polynomial shows a visible pattern or is a quadratic you can split into two brackets, try the patterns in a fixed order: a common factor, a difference of squares, a sum or difference of cubes, then grouping. For $x^2+px+q$, find numbers $r$ and $s$ with $r+s=p$ and $rs=q$, which gives $(x+r)(x+s)$.
$$a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b),\qquad a^3\mp b^3=(a\mp b)(a^2\pm ab+b^2)$$
Factoring also links roots to coefficients. If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of $ax^2+bx+c$, then
$$\alpha+\beta=-\frac{b}{a},\qquad \alpha\beta=\frac{c}{a},\qquad \alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta$$

The core intuition here is that factors expose the roots and let you cancel in fractions. Comparing the factored form with the expanded form gives the coefficient relations above.

*Example:* Factor $x^3+64$ by taking $a=x$ and $b=4$. Separately, the roots of $x^2-5x+2$ have sum $5$ and product $2$.
$$x^3+64=(x+4)(x^2-4x+16),\qquad \alpha^2+\beta^2=25-4=21$$

*Trap:* A sum of squares such as $a^2+b^2$ has no real factors, so do not force it. Also keep the minus sign in $-\frac{b}{a}$.

*Check:* Expand your answer and confirm it matches the original polynomial. Here $x^2-4x+16$ has a negative discriminant, so the factoring stops there.

name: Polynomial division
teach:
When you divide a polynomial by a bracket like $x-c$, or need a root of a cubic or higher polynomial, the remainder of $p(x)$ divided by $x-c$ is simply $p(c)$. To find roots, list the candidates $\pm\frac{\text{factor of the constant}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}$ and test them. Then divide by the root you found using the coefficient method of the example.
$$p(x)=(x-c)\,q(x)+p(c)$$

The core intuition here is that if $p(c)=0$ then $x-c$ is a factor, so each root you find removes one degree. The remainder theorem gives the remainder with no long division at all.

*Example:* Divide $p(x)=x^3-5x^2+2x+8$ by $x-4$. The remainder is $p(4)=64-80+8+8=0$. For the quotient, bring down each coefficient in turn, adding $4$ times the previous result.
$$1,\ \ -5+4=-1,\ \ 2-4=-2,\ \ 8-8=0 \;\Longrightarrow\; q(x)=x^2-x-2$$

*Trap:* Using $c$ when the divisor is $x+c$. That divisor needs the value $-c$.

*Check:* Multiply quotient by divisor and add the remainder to recover the original.

name: Rational expressions
teach:
When an expression or equation has fractions whose numerators and denominators are polynomials, factor every numerator and denominator, cancel shared factors, then combine over a common denominator. For an equation, multiply through by the common denominator and solve. Then discard any root that makes an original denominator zero.
$$\frac{A}{B}+\frac{C}{D}=\frac{AD+CB}{BD}$$

The core intuition here is that only common factors cancel, never common terms. Factoring first reveals which factors can go and which values are forbidden.

*Example:* Simplify $\frac{x^2-16}{x^2+x-20}$ for $x\ne 4,-5$.
$$\frac{(x-4)(x+4)}{(x-4)(x+5)}=\frac{x+4}{x+5}$$

*Trap:* Cancelling terms instead of factors. The fraction $\frac{x^2+4}{x}$ is not $x+4$.

*Check:* Pick a number such as $x=0$ and confirm both forms give the same value.

name: Exponent and radical rules
teach:
When an expression has exponents that are negative, fractional or stacked, or has radicals you need to simplify or rationalize, reduce everything to one base and apply the rules. To clear a radical denominator, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate, so that $(\sqrt u-\sqrt v)(\sqrt u+\sqrt v)=u-v$.
$$a^ma^n=a^{m+n},\quad (a^m)^n=a^{mn},\quad a^{-m}=\frac1{a^m},\quad a^{m/n}=\sqrt[n]{a^m}$$

The core intuition here is that an exponent counts repeated multiplication, so the rules follow from counting factors. Fractional powers extend the same rules to roots, and negative powers extend them to reciprocals, so one set of rules covers every case.

*Example:* Rationalize $\frac{6}{\sqrt7+1}$.
$$\frac{6(\sqrt7-1)}{(\sqrt7+1)(\sqrt7-1)}=\frac{6(\sqrt7-1)}{6}=\sqrt7-1$$

*Trap:* Treating $(a+b)^n$ as $a^n+b^n$. Powers distribute over products, never over sums. Also watch $(-a)^2$ versus $-a^2$.

*Check:* Estimate both forms. Here $\frac{6}{3.65}\approx1.64$ and $\sqrt7-1\approx1.65$.

name: Absolute value and inequalities
teach:
When an inequality contains an absolute value, rewrite it as a pair of inequalities, taking $b>0$. When it is a fraction or polynomial whose sign changes across its zeros, mark the zeros of the numerator and denominator, test one point in each interval, then decide the endpoints.
$$|u|=b\iff u=\pm b,\qquad |u|<b\iff -b<u<b,\qquad |u|>b\iff u<-b \text{ or } u>b$$

The core intuition here is that $|u|$ is the distance of $u$ from zero, so $|u|<b$ means $u$ is within $b$ of zero. Signs only change at zeros and at undefined points, so testing one point per interval is enough.

*Example:* Solve $\frac{x-3}{x+1}\le 0$. The marked points are $3$ and $-1$, and the point $3$ is included because the fraction equals zero there.
$$-1<x\le 3$$

*Trap:* Do not multiply by an expression of unknown sign, and never include a zero of the denominator.

*Check:* Test a point inside and a point outside your answer.

name: Function notation and domain
teach:
When a formula is written as $f(x)$, or you are asked which inputs a formula accepts, evaluate by replacing every $x$ with the input, in brackets, and simplifying. For the domain, exclude inputs that cause a zero denominator or a negative value under an even root. For a piecewise function, use the branch whose condition holds.
$$f(a)=\text{the formula with } x \text{ replaced by } a$$

The core intuition here is that a function assigns each input exactly one output. The domain is the set of inputs where the formula makes sense.

*Example:* Find the domain of $f(x)=\frac{\sqrt{3-x}}{x+2}$. The root needs $3-x\ge0$, and the denominator needs $x\ne-2$.
$$x\le 3 \text{ and } x\ne -2$$

*Trap:* Writing $f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b)$, which is almost never true. For $f(x)=x^2$, $f(2+3)=25$ but $f(2)+f(3)=13$.

*Check:* Feed one value from your domain and one from outside it into the formula.

name: Composition and inverse
teach:
When two functions are applied one after the other, or you must undo a function to recover its input, remember that in $f\circ g$ you apply $g$ first. To find $f^{-1}$, write $y=f(x)$, swap $x$ and $y$, then solve for $y$. Only one-to-one functions have inverses.
$$(f\circ g)(x)=f(g(x))$$

The core intuition here is that composition feeds the output of the inner function into the outer one, like two machines in a row. An inverse runs the machine backwards, which only works if no two different inputs share the same output.

*Example:* Find the inverse of $f(x)=\frac{x}{2}+5$. Swap and solve, which gives $f^{-1}(x)=2x-10$.
$$x=\frac{y}{2}+5 \;\Longrightarrow\; y=2(x-5)$$

*Trap:* Reading $f^{-1}(x)$ as the reciprocal $\frac1{f(x)}$, which is a different thing. Also assuming $f\circ g=g\circ f$, when the order of composition matters.

*Check:* Confirm $f(f^{-1}(x))=x$. Here $\frac{2x-10}{2}+5=x$.

name: Graph transformations
teach:
When a graph is shifted, stretched or reflected, or a symmetry of $f$ is asked about, read $y=a\,f(x-h)+k$ from the inside out. It shifts right by $h$ and up by $k$, and it stretches vertically by $|a|$. A negative $a$ reflects in the $x$-axis, and $f(-x)$ reflects in the $y$-axis. A function is even if $f(-x)=f(x)$ and odd if $f(-x)=-f(x)$.
$$y=a\,f(x-h)+k$$

The core intuition here is that changes made inside the brackets act on inputs, so they move the graph sideways and in the opposite direction to what the sign suggests. Changes made outside act on outputs.

*Example:* Describe $y=-2f(x+1)+3$, where $h=-1$.
$$\text{left } 1,\ \text{stretch } 2,\ \text{flip over the } x\text{-axis},\ \text{up } 3$$

*Trap:* Thinking $f(x+2)$ moves right. The graph reaches each old value two units earlier, so it moves left.

*Check:* Follow one point of the original graph through each change.

name: Coordinate geometry
teach:
When a question involves points, lines or circles in the plane, use these formulas. The distance and the slope come from two points, the midpoint averages the coordinates, and a line through $(x_1,y_1)$ with slope $m$ is $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$. To read a circle from an expanded equation, complete the square in $x$ and in $y$.
$$d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2},\qquad m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1},\qquad (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$$

The core intuition here is that every formula comes from the Pythagorean theorem or from rise over run. A circle with center $(h,k)$ is the set of points at a fixed distance $r$ from that center.

*Example:* Find the center and radius of $x^2+y^2+4x-6y-12=0$. Completing both squares gives the center $(-2,3)$ and radius $5$.
$$(x+2)^2+(y-3)^2=12+4+9=25$$

*Trap:* A vertical line has undefined slope, not slope $0$. Only a horizontal line has slope $0$.

*Check:* The right side, the radius squared, must be positive.

name: Plane and solid geometry
teach:
When a problem gives lengths or angles of triangles, circles or solids and asks for an area, volume or missing length, recall the standard formulas and use similarity. In a right triangle with legs $a,b$ and hypotenuse $c$, Pythagoras applies. For a circle or cylinder, $r$ is the radius, and for a cone or cylinder, $h$ is the height.
$$a^2+b^2=c^2,\qquad A_{\text{circle}}=\pi r^2,\qquad V_{\text{cone}}=\tfrac13\pi r^2h,\qquad V_{\text{cyl}}=\pi r^2h$$

The core intuition here is that nearly every plane problem reduces to right triangles or circles. Scaling lengths by $k$ scales areas by $k^2$ and volumes by $k^3$, which lets you skip the full formula.

*Example:* A cone has radius $3$ and height $4$, and you need its volume. The slant height $5$ is not needed.
$$V=\tfrac13\pi(3)^2(4)=12\pi$$

*Trap:* Using the diameter where the formula needs the radius.

*Check:* Compare with a simpler solid. The cone has one third of the volume of the cylinder around it, which is $36\pi$.

name: Unit circle values
teach:
When an angle needs an exact sine, cosine or tangent, it is usually a multiple of $30^\circ$ or $45^\circ$, which is $\frac{\pi}{6}$ or $\frac{\pi}{4}$ in radians. Find the reference angle, the acute angle it makes with the $x$-axis, and read its value from the table. Then apply the quadrant sign. Sine is positive in quadrants I and II, cosine in I and IV, and tangent in I and III.
$$\sin30^\circ=\tfrac12,\quad \sin45^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2},\quad \sin60^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$$
Cosine runs the same table in reverse order, and $\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$.

The core intuition here is that on the unit circle the point at angle $\theta$ is $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$. Every angle shares its values, up to sign, with an acute reference angle.

*Example:* Find $\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}$. The angle is in quadrant II with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{6}$.
$$\cos\tfrac{5\pi}{6}=-\cos\tfrac{\pi}{6}=-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$$

*Trap:* Taking the value from the table and forgetting the quadrant sign.

*Check:* The cosine is the $x$-coordinate, so it must be negative in quadrant II.

name: Trig identities
teach:
When a trig expression needs simplifying, or one trig value is given and another is asked for, rewrite everything in $\sin$ and $\cos$ and then use the identities. Given one value, solve the Pythagorean identity for the other and choose the sign from the quadrant.
$$\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1,\qquad 1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta,\qquad \sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$$
$$\cos2\theta=\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta=2\cos^2\theta-1$$

The core intuition here is that the point $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ lies on the unit circle, so the Pythagorean identity links sine and cosine. Every other identity follows from it.

*Example:* If $\cos\theta=-\frac{8}{17}$ and $\theta$ is in quadrant II, find $\sin\theta$. The sign is positive because sine is positive in quadrant II.
$$\sin^2\theta=1-\tfrac{64}{289}=\tfrac{225}{289}\;\Longrightarrow\;\sin\theta=\tfrac{15}{17}$$

*Trap:* Taking the square root and skipping the quadrant check, which can give the wrong sign.

*Check:* The sum of the squares of your two values must equal $1$.

name: Trig equations
teach:
When a trig equation must be solved on a given interval, isolate one trig function and find the reference angle. Then list every angle in the interval that gives that value. Add whole periods for a general solution, which are $2\pi k$ for sine and cosine and $\pi k$ for tangent. For a multiple angle such as $\cos2x$, solve for $2x$ on the stretched interval and then halve. For a trig quadratic, substitute $u=\sin x$ and solve for $u$ first. Here $\alpha$ is the reference angle and $k$ is any integer.
$$\sin x=c \;\Longrightarrow\; x=\alpha+2\pi k \ \text{ or }\ x=\pi-\alpha+2\pi k$$

The core intuition here is that trig functions repeat, so one value of the function is hit by several angles. A single answer is almost never the whole answer.

*Example:* Solve $2\sin x=\sqrt3$ on $[0,2\pi)$. Then $\sin x=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, with reference angle $\frac\pi3$.
$$x=\tfrac{\pi}{3}\ \text{ or }\ x=\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$$

*Trap:* Listing only the principal angle, or using the period of sine for tangent.

*Check:* Sine is positive in quadrants I and II, which matches both answers.

name: Trig graphs
teach:
When you sketch or read a graph of the form $y=A\sin(Bx-C)+D$, or the cosine or tangent version, read the constants in this order. The amplitude is $|A|$, the period is $\frac{2\pi}{|B|}$, or $\frac{\pi}{|B|}$ for tangent, the midline is $y=D$, and the phase shift is $\frac CB$ to the right.
$$\text{range}=[\,D-|A|,\ D+|A|\,]$$

The core intuition here is that each constant is a transformation of the basic wave. The value $A$ stretches vertically, $B$ squeezes horizontally, $C$ shifts and $D$ lifts, so each can be read off separately.

*Example:* Analyse $y=2\cos(3x-\pi)-1$.
$$\text{amplitude }2,\quad \text{period }\tfrac{2\pi}{3},\quad \text{shift }\tfrac{\pi}{3}\text{ right},\quad \text{range }[-3,1]$$

*Trap:* Shifting by $C$ instead of $\frac CB$. Factor out $B$ first, since $\sin(Bx-C)=\sin\big(B(x-\frac CB)\big)$.

*Check:* A sine or cosine wave touches its maximum and minimum exactly once per period, so the range must match the amplitude and midline you found.

name: Inverse trig
teach:
When you need an angle from a trig value, or a trig function of an inverse trig function, start from the range of the inverse. To evaluate a trig function of an inverse, draw a right triangle with that angle, fill in two sides from the given ratio, and find the third with the Pythagorean theorem. For $\arccos(\cos\theta)$ with $\theta$ outside the range, find the angle in the range with the same cosine.
$$\arcsin:\ [-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2],\qquad \arccos:\ [0,\pi],\qquad \arctan:\ (-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2)$$

The core intuition here is that trig functions repeat, so they fail to be one-to-one. Each inverse restricts to one fixed range so that it returns a single, well-defined angle.

*Example:* Find $\tan\big(\arccos\frac{8}{17}\big)$. The angle has adjacent side $8$ and hypotenuse $17$, so the opposite side is $15$.
$$\tan\big(\arccos\tfrac{8}{17}\big)=\tfrac{15}{8}$$

*Trap:* Writing $\arccos(\cos\theta)=\theta$ for every $\theta$. It holds only for $\theta$ in $[0,\pi]$.

*Check:* The cosine is positive, so the angle lies in $[0,\frac\pi2)$ and its tangent must be positive.

name: Law of sines and cosines
teach:
When a triangle has no right angle and you know three parts, including at least one side, choose the law that fits the data. Take sides $a,b,c$ opposite angles $A,B,C$. Use the law of cosines when you know all three sides or two sides and the angle between them. Use the law of sines when you know an angle and its opposite side plus one more part.
$$c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C,\qquad \frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C}$$

The core intuition here is that the law of cosines generalizes the Pythagorean theorem, with a correction term that vanishes when $C=90^\circ$. The law of sines says each side is proportional to the sine of its opposite angle.

*Example:* A triangle has $a=4$, $b=6$ and angle $C=120^\circ$ between them, and you need $c$.
$$c^2=16+36-48\cos120^\circ=52+24=76,\qquad c=2\sqrt{19}$$

*Trap:* In the SSA case there can be two triangles, because $\arcsin$ returns only one of two possible angles. Test $180^\circ-B$ as well.

*Check:* The longest side must lie opposite the largest angle.

name: Exponentials and logs
teach:
When an expression has exponentials or logarithms, or you must free a variable from an exponent, use these rules, which hold for positive $x$ and $y$ and a base $b\ne1$. To bring an exponent down, take the log of both sides. To change base, use the last formula. Keep the base visible in every line you write.
$$\log_b(xy)=\log_bx+\log_by,\qquad \log_b\tfrac xy=\log_bx-\log_by,\qquad \log_b(x^r)=r\log_bx$$
$$\log_b b^x=x,\qquad e^{\ln x}=x,\qquad \log_bx=\frac{\ln x}{\ln b}$$

The core intuition here is that a logarithm is the inverse of an exponential. So $\log_b x$ asks which power of $b$ gives $x$, and the log rules mirror the exponent rules.

*Example:* Evaluate $\log_2 40-\log_2 5$.
$$\log_2\tfrac{40}{5}=\log_2 8=3$$

*Trap:* Writing $\log(x+y)=\log x+\log y$. Logs split products, never sums.

*Check:* Rewrite the answer as a power: $2^3=8$, which matches the quotient $\frac{40}{5}$.

name: Log and exponential equations
teach:
When an equation has the variable in an exponent or inside a logarithm, combine the logs into one, or rewrite both sides with the same base, then compare. Solve the resulting equation. Then substitute each root into the original and keep it only if every log argument is positive.
$$\log_b A=C \;\Longleftrightarrow\; A=b^{C}$$

The core intuition here is that logs and exponentials undo each other, so applying one to both sides turns the equation into an algebraic one. A log accepts only positive arguments, so some algebraic roots are fake.

*Example:* Solve $\log_3(x)+\log_3(x-2)=1$. Reject $x=-1$ because it makes $\log_3 x$ undefined, so the answer is $x=3$.
$$x(x-2)=3 \;\Longrightarrow\; x^2-2x-3=0 \;\Longrightarrow\; x=3 \text{ or } x=-1$$

*Trap:* Keeping a root that makes a log argument zero or negative.

*Check:* Substitute the survivor into the original equation.

name: Arithmetic and geometric sequences
teach:
When a list of numbers has a constant difference or a constant ratio and you need a term or a sum, use the closed forms. For an arithmetic list with difference $d$, and for a geometric list with ratio $r$, the $n$th term is $a_n$ and the sum of the first $n$ terms is $S_n$. When $|r|<1$ the infinite geometric sum is $S_\infty=\frac{a_1}{1-r}$.
$$a_n=a_1+(n-1)d,\quad S_n=\frac{n(a_1+a_n)}{2};\qquad a_n=a_1r^{n-1},\quad S_n=\frac{a_1(1-r^n)}{1-r}$$

The core intuition here is that a constant difference grows the terms linearly and a constant ratio grows them exponentially. Each pattern has a closed form, so you never add term by term.

*Example:* Sum the first $10$ terms of $7,10,13,\ldots$ Here $a_1=7$ and $d=3$, so $a_{10}=34$.
$$S_{10}=\frac{10(7+34)}{2}=205$$

*Trap:* Using the arithmetic sum on a geometric sequence, or miscounting $n$.

*Check:* The sum of an arithmetic list equals the average of the ends times the number of terms.

name: Sigma notation and binomial theorem
teach:
When a sum has an index like $\sum_{k=1}^{n}$, or you expand a binomial power such as $(a+b)^n$, use the formulas below. Here $\binom nk=\frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}$, and $n!$ is the product of the integers from $1$ to $n$. Split sums term by term and pull out constants. When the brackets hold powers of $x$, find the $k$ that gives the exponent you want, and read the coefficient from that term.
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=\frac{n(n+1)}{2},\qquad \sum_{k=1}^{n}k^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6},\qquad \binom nk a^{n-k}b^k$$

The core intuition here is that sigma notation is a compact list of terms. In a binomial power, each term picks $b$ from $k$ brackets and $a$ from the rest, and $\binom nk$ counts the ways.

*Example:* Find the coefficient of $x^3$ in $(2+x)^5$.
$$\binom53\,2^{2}=10\cdot4=40$$

*Trap:* Starting the index at $0$ when the sum starts at $1$, or forgetting the power on the constant, here $2^2$.

*Check:* The coefficients of $(1+x)^n$ sum to $2^n$.

name: Logic and sets
teach:
When a statement uses "for all", "there exists" or "if then", or a problem counts the elements of unions and intersections, negate and count with these rules. The converse $q\to p$ is not equivalent to $p\to q$. A set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets.
$$\neg\forall x\,P\equiv\exists x\,\neg P,\qquad (p\to q)\equiv(\neg q\to\neg p),\qquad |A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|$$

The core intuition here is that negating a statement correctly is mechanical. Every quantifier flips and the predicate gets negated, and the contrapositive says the same thing as the original.

*Example:* In a class of $30$, let $A$ be the $18$ who study French and $B$ the $14$ who study Spanish. Everyone studies at least one of them. How many study both?
$$30=18+14-|A\cap B| \;\Longrightarrow\; |A\cap B|=2$$

*Trap:* Treating the converse as the contrapositive.

*Check:* The count of "both" cannot exceed the smaller set.

name: Proof methods
teach:
When you must choose how to prove a claim, or judge whether a given argument really proves it, match the method to the statement $p\to q$. A direct proof starts from $p$ and reaches $q$. A contrapositive proof starts from $\neg q$ and reaches $\neg p$. Contradiction assumes $p$ together with $\neg q$ and derives something false. One example proves an existence claim, and a single counterexample disproves a universal claim.
$$\text{direct: } p\Rightarrow\cdots\Rightarrow q;\qquad \text{contrapositive: } \neg q\Rightarrow\cdots\Rightarrow\neg p$$

The core intuition here is that each method is a different route to the same conclusion. The right choice makes the proof short, and a wrong one proves nothing.

*Example:* Prove that if $3n+2$ is odd then $n$ is odd. Use the contrapositive: assume $n$ is even, so $n=2m$. Then $3n+2$ is even, so it is not odd.
$$3n+2=6m+2=2(3m+1)$$

*Trap:* Assuming the conclusion, or trying to prove a universal claim from examples.

*Check:* Ask what the proof assumed and what it reached, and confirm that these match the method.

name: Induction
teach:
When a claim $P(n)$ must be shown for every integer $n$ from some starting value $n_0$, use induction. First check the base case $P(n_0)$, testing small $n$ if you are not sure where the claim starts. Then assume $P(k)$ for some $k\ge n_0$, called the inductive hypothesis, and prove $P(k+1)$, using $P(k)$ somewhere in the argument.
$$P(n_0)\ \text{true};\qquad P(k)\Rightarrow P(k+1)\ \text{for every } k\ge n_0$$

The core intuition here is that induction works like falling dominoes. If the first one falls and each one knocks over the next, they all fall.

*Example:* Show $1+2+\cdots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$. The base $n=1$ gives $1=1$. For the step, add $k+1$ to both sides of $P(k)$, which yields $P(k+1)$.
$$\frac{k(k+1)}{2}+(k+1)=\frac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}$$

*Trap:* Proving the step without a base case, or never using the hypothesis.

*Check:* The target for $P(k+1)$ is the formula with $k+1$ in place of $n$.

name: Algebraic limits
teach:
When you need $\lim_{x\to a}$ of a rational or radical expression, always substitute $x=a$ first, since that tells you whether any work is needed. If you get $\frac00$, factor the top and bottom, or multiply by the conjugate for a root, and cancel the common factor. Then substitute again.
$$\lim_{x\to a}\frac{(x-a)\,g(x)}{(x-a)\,h(x)}=\lim_{x\to a}\frac{g(x)}{h(x)}$$

The core intuition here is that the form $\frac00$ means numerator and denominator share a hidden factor that vanishes at $a$. The limit looks at nearby values, where $x\ne a$, so that factor can be cancelled.

*Example:* Find $\lim_{x\to4}\frac{\sqrt{x}-2}{x-4}$ by multiplying by the conjugate $\sqrt x+2$.
$$\frac{x-4}{(x-4)(\sqrt x+2)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt x+2}\;\longrightarrow\;\frac14$$

*Trap:* Cancel factors, never terms. Also, a nonzero number over zero is not $\frac00$. That case means the limit is infinite or does not exist.

*Check:* Evaluate the original at a number close to $a$, such as $x=4.01$.

name: Special limits and squeeze
teach:
When a limit has $\sin$, $1-\cos$, $e^x-1$ or $\ln(1+x)$ with a variable tending to $0$, rewrite the expression so the inside of the function matches the denominator. Then apply the standard limits as $u\to0$, and write $\tan u$ as $\frac{\sin u}{\cos u}$ when it appears. If a bounded factor such as $\sin\frac1x$ multiplies a term that tends to zero, squeeze the expression between two functions with the same limit.
$$\frac{\sin u}{u}\to1,\qquad \frac{1-\cos u}{u^2}\to\frac12,\qquad \frac{e^u-1}{u}\to1,\qquad \frac{\ln(1+u)}{u}\to1$$

The core intuition here is that near zero these functions behave like simple polynomials. For example $\sin u\approx u$ and $1-\cos u\approx\frac{u^2}{2}$, so their ratios settle at fixed numbers.

*Example:* Find $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin 5x}{2x}$ by writing it as $\frac52\cdot\frac{\sin5x}{5x}$.
$$\tfrac52\cdot1=\tfrac52$$

*Trap:* The argument of the sine must match the denominator exactly, so $\frac{\sin 5x}{2x}$ does not tend to $1$.

*Check:* For small $x$, $\sin5x\approx5x$, which agrees.

name: Continuity
teach:
When a function has a hole or a split definition, or a parameter must be chosen so that the graph has no break, verify three things at $x=a$. For a piecewise function, compute the left and right limits and set them equal to each other and to $f(a)$, then solve for the parameter. For a hole, cancel the common factor and set $f(a)$ equal to the limit.
$$f(a)\text{ is defined},\qquad \lim_{x\to a}f(x)\text{ exists},\qquad \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a)$$

The core intuition here is that continuity means you can draw the graph through the point without lifting the pen. That needs a value, a limit, and agreement between them.

*Example:* Choose $k$ so that $f$ is continuous at $1$, where $f(x)=x^2+3$ for $x<1$ and $f(x)=kx$ for $x\ge1$.
$$\lim_{x\to1^-}f=1+3=4,\qquad f(1)=k\;\Longrightarrow\;k=4$$

*Trap:* Matching only one side, when continuity needs both sides to agree with $f(a)$. Continuity also does not imply differentiability, since $|x|$ is continuous at $0$ but has a corner.

*Check:* Substitute your parameter into both branches at $a$.

name: Derivative from definition
teach:
When a derivative is requested from the definition, or a corner such as $|x|$ at $0$ defeats the usual rules, write the difference quotient, expand, cancel the factor $h$, then let $h\to0$. A limit already in this form is $f'(a)$, so read off $f$ and $a$. For a root, multiply by the conjugate. At a corner, compute the limit from the left and from the right, since the derivative exists only if they agree.
$$f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$$

The core intuition here is that the derivative is the slope of the tangent. It is found as the limit of slopes of secant lines through two nearby points a distance $h$ apart.

*Example:* Find $f'(a)$ for $f(x)=2x^3-x$.
$$\frac{2(a+h)^3-(a+h)-2a^3+a}{h}=\frac{6a^2h+6ah^2+2h^3-h}{h}=6a^2+6ah+2h^2-1\;\longrightarrow\;6a^2-1$$

*Trap:* Forgetting to subtract $f(a)$, or dividing by $a$ instead of $h$.

*Check:* The slope should match a power-rule check, since the derivative of $2x^3-x$ is $6x^2-1$.

name: Power, product, quotient rules
teach:
When a function is a sum, product or quotient of powers and simple pieces, with no function inside another, differentiate sums term by term and use these rules for products and quotients of functions $u$ and $v$. The power rule holds for any real $n$, including negatives and fractions, so rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first. Evaluate at the given point only after you simplify.
$$(uv)'=u'v+uv',\qquad \left(\frac uv\right)'=\frac{u'v-uv'}{v^2},\qquad (x^n)'=nx^{n-1}$$

The core intuition here is that the rules turn one difficult limit into routine steps. The product rule has two terms because both factors change at once.

*Example:* Differentiate $\frac{x^2}{x-1}$, where $u=x^2$ and $v=x-1$.
$$\frac{2x(x-1)-x^2(1)}{(x-1)^2}=\frac{x^2-2x}{(x-1)^2}$$

*Trap:* The product rule is not $u'v'$. In the quotient numerator the order matters, because it is $u'v-uv'$.

*Check:* At $x=3$ the formula gives $\frac34$. The function values $4.5$ at $x=3$ and about $4.5075$ at $x=3.01$ give the same slope.

name: Chain rule
teach:
When one function sits inside another, as in $(3x+1)^5$, $\sin(x^2)$ or $e^{x^2}$, differentiate the outer function $f$ and leave the inner function $g$ alone inside it. Then multiply by the derivative of the inner function. For several layers, peel from the outside in and multiply each factor.
$$\frac{d}{dx}f(g(x))=f'(g(x))\cdot g'(x)$$

The core intuition here is that the output rate is the outer rate times the inner rate. If $y$ changes $3$ times as fast as $u$, and $u$ changes $2$ times as fast as $x$, then $y$ changes $6$ times as fast as $x$.

*Example:* Differentiate $\sin^3(2x)$, whose layers are cube, sine, then $2x$.
$$3\sin^2(2x)\cdot\cos(2x)\cdot 2=6\sin^2(2x)\cos(2x)$$

*Trap:* Dropping the inner derivative, or evaluating the outer derivative at $x$ instead of at $g(x)$.

*Check:* Count the layers in the function and the factors in your answer. They should match.

name: Transcendental derivatives
teach:
When the function involves $e^x$, $\ln x$, $a^x$, trig functions or inverse trig functions, use this table. If the input is more than a bare $x$, multiply by the derivative of the input, which is the chain rule.
$$(e^x)'=e^x,\quad (a^x)'=a^x\ln a,\quad (\ln x)'=\tfrac1x,\quad (\sin x)'=\cos x,\quad (\cos x)'=-\sin x$$
$$(\tan x)'=\sec^2x,\quad (\arcsin x)'=\tfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}},\quad (\arctan x)'=\tfrac{1}{1+x^2}$$

The core intuition here is that in these functions the variable is not in the base of a power, so the power rule does not apply. They are standard results to memorize, and the chain rule handles every composite.

*Example:* Differentiate $\ln(x^2+1)$.
$$\frac{1}{x^2+1}\cdot2x=\frac{2x}{x^2+1}$$

*Trap:* Using the power rule on $a^x$ to get $xa^{x-1}$. In $a^x$ the variable is in the exponent.

*Check:* At $x=1$ the formula gives $1$. The values $\ln2$ at $x=1$ and $\ln2.0201$ at $x=1.01$ differ by about $0.01$, which agrees.

name: Implicit differentiation
teach:
When $x$ and $y$ are tangled in one equation, such as $xy+y^2=5$, and solving for $y$ is hard, differentiate both sides with respect to $x$. Multiply the derivative of every $y$ term by $y'$, and use the product rule on terms like $xy$. Then collect the $y'$ terms and solve. The answer may contain both $x$ and $y$, so put in the point's two coordinates at the end.
$$\frac{d}{dx}\,y^n=n\,y^{n-1}\,y'$$

The core intuition here is that $y$ is an unknown function of $x$. So any expression in $y$ needs the chain rule, which produces a factor $\frac{dy}{dx}$.

*Example:* Find $y'$ for $xy+y^2=5$.
$$y+xy'+2yy'=0\;\Longrightarrow\;y'=-\frac{y}{x+2y}$$

*Trap:* Forgetting the $y'$ on a $y$ term, or missing the product rule on $xy$.

*Check:* The point $(4,1)$ lies on the curve and gives $y'=-\frac16$. Since $y(x+y)=5$, $y$ must fall as $x$ rises, so the sign is right.

name: Logarithmic differentiation
teach:
When a function is a product or quotient with many factors, or has the variable in both the base and the exponent, as in $x^x$, take $\ln$ of both sides and expand with the log rules. Differentiate implicitly, then multiply by $y$ to remove the fraction.
$$\frac{y'}{y}=\frac{d}{dx}\ln y\;\Longrightarrow\;y'=y\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\ln y$$

The core intuition here is that taking logs turns products into sums and powers into multiples. Sums are far easier to differentiate than long products.

*Example:* Differentiate $y=x^{\sin x}$ for $x>0$. Taking logs and differentiating gives the line below, and multiplying by $y$ gives $y'=x^{\sin x}\left(\cos x\ln x+\frac{\sin x}{x}\right)$.
$$\ln y=\sin x\,\ln x\;\Longrightarrow\;\frac{y'}{y}=\cos x\ln x+\frac{\sin x}{x}$$

*Trap:* Leaving the log of a product unexpanded, or forgetting the final factor $y$.

*Check:* The function must be positive where you take the log. Use $\ln|y|$ if it can be negative.

name: L'Hopital's rule
teach:
When a limit gives $\frac00$ or $\frac\infty\infty$ after substitution and the top and bottom are differentiable, differentiate the numerator and the denominator separately, then take the limit again. Repeat if the form is still indeterminate. For $0\cdot\infty$, rewrite the product as a quotient first. For $1^\infty$, take the log.
$$\lim\frac{f}{g}=\lim\frac{f'}{g'}$$

The core intuition here is that near the point both functions look like straight lines. So their ratio is the ratio of their slopes.

*Example:* Find $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{2x}-1-2x}{x^2}$, where substitution gives $\frac00$. The first step still gave $\frac00$, so the rule was applied twice.
$$\lim\frac{2e^{2x}-2}{2x}=\lim\frac{4e^{2x}}{2}=2$$

*Trap:* Applying the quotient rule to the fraction, or skipping the check that the form is indeterminate.

*Check:* Confirm the form is $\frac00$ or $\frac\infty\infty$ at every step.

name: Related rates
teach:
When several quantities change with time, a formula links them, and you know some rates and want another, draw the picture and write the equation linking the quantities. Differentiate with respect to $t$ using the chain rule. Only now substitute the given values, then solve for the unknown rate.
$$\frac{d}{dt}f(x)=f'(x)\,\frac{dx}{dt}$$

The core intuition here is that if two quantities are tied by an equation, their rates of change are tied too. Differentiating the equation with respect to time gives that tie.

*Example:* The radius of a circle grows at $4$ units per second. How fast is the area growing when $r=7$?
$$A=\pi r^2\;\Longrightarrow\;\frac{dA}{dt}=2\pi r\frac{dr}{dt}=2\pi(7)(4)=56\pi$$

*Trap:* Substituting the numbers before differentiating, which freezes the quantity that should change.

*Check:* The units of the answer are area per second, which is units squared per second.

name: Optimization
teach:
When a quantity must be made as large or as small as possible, usually under a constraint, write the objective, use the constraint to reduce it to one variable, and state the domain. Find the critical points, where $f'=0$ or $f'$ is undefined. Then compare the values there and at the endpoints.
$$f'(x)=0\ \text{ or undefined},\qquad \text{answer}=\max\ \text{or}\ \min\ \text{of } f \text{ at all candidates}$$

The core intuition here is that at a smooth peak or valley the tangent is flat, so the derivative is zero there. Endpoints and corners are the other candidates.

*Example:* A rectangle has perimeter $24$ and one side $x$, so the other side is $12-x$. Maximize the area. At the endpoints $x=0$ and $x=12$ the area is $0$.
$$A=x(12-x),\qquad A'=12-2x=0\;\Longrightarrow\;x=6,\quad A=36$$

*Trap:* Skipping the domain, or ignoring the endpoints of a closed interval.

*Check:* The answer must satisfy the original constraint.

name: Curve shape
teach:
When you sketch a graph, or find where a function rises, falls, bends up or bends down, find where $f'$ and $f''$ are zero or undefined, then test the sign of each in the intervals between. A local extremum is a sign change of $f'$, and an inflection point is a sign change of $f''$.
$$f'>0\Rightarrow\text{increasing},\quad f'<0\Rightarrow\text{decreasing},\quad f''>0\Rightarrow\text{concave up},\quad f''<0\Rightarrow\text{concave down}$$

The core intuition here is that the first derivative is the slope and the second derivative is how the slope changes. Together they describe the whole shape.

*Example:* Analyse $f(x)=x^3-6x^2$, where $f'=3x^2-12x=3x(x-4)$ and $f''=6x-12$. So there is a local max at $0$, a local min at $4$, and an inflection point at $2$.
$$f'<0\text{ on }(0,4),\quad f''=0\text{ at }x=2$$

*Trap:* Calling every zero of $f'$ an extremum. With no sign change it is neither.

*Check:* Between a local max and a local min, the function must decrease.

name: Rolle and Mean Value Theorem
teach:
When a claim says a derivative takes a certain value somewhere in an interval, or you must find such a point, first verify that $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. Then there is a $c$ in $(a,b)$ with the formula below. If also $f(a)=f(b)$, the right side is $0$, which is Rolle's theorem. Solve for $c$ and check it lies inside the interval.
$$f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$$

The core intuition here is that a smooth path from $A$ to $B$ must at some moment move at its average speed. Rolle's theorem is the special case with equal ends, where the path must pause.

*Example:* For $f(x)=x^3-x$ on $[0,2]$ the average slope is $\frac{6-0}{2}=3$. The root $-\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$ lies outside the interval, so it is rejected.
$$3c^2-1=3\;\Longrightarrow\;c=\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\approx1.15$$

*Trap:* Skipping the hypotheses, because the conclusion can fail without them, as for $|x|$ on $[-1,1]$.

*Check:* The value of $c$ is strictly between $a$ and $b$.

name: Basic antiderivatives
teach:
When you must undo a derivative of a sum of powers, exponentials or standard trig terms, with nothing hidden inside, integrate term by term. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first. When the input is $kx$ rather than $x$, divide by $k$, so that $\int\cos kx\,dx=\frac{\sin kx}{k}+C$ and $\int\sin kx\,dx=-\frac{\cos kx}{k}+C$. For a definite integral, compute $F(b)-F(a)$.
$$\int x^n\,dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C\ (n\ne-1),\quad \int\frac{dx}{x}=\ln|x|+C,\quad \int e^{kx}dx=\frac{e^{kx}}{k}+C$$

The core intuition here is that an antiderivative $F$ of $f$ satisfies $F'=f$, so each derivative rule read backwards is an integration rule. The constant $C$ appears because constants differentiate to zero.

*Example:* Find $\int\left(6x^2-\frac{3}{x}+e^{-2x}\right)dx$.
$$2x^3-3\ln|x|-\tfrac12e^{-2x}+C$$

*Trap:* Dividing by the old power instead of the new one, or forgetting the factor $\frac1k$ when the input is $kx$.

*Check:* Differentiate your answer term by term. You must get the original integrand back exactly.

name: Substitution
teach:
When the integrand looks like $f(g(x))\,g'(x)$, a function of an inner piece times that piece's derivative up to a constant, set $u=g(x)$ and $du=g'(x)\,dx$, and rewrite everything in $u$. For a definite integral, convert the limits too. If $du$ misses a constant factor, divide by it. Finish in $u$, then substitute back if the integral was indefinite.
$$\int f(g(x))\,g'(x)\,dx=\int f(u)\,du,\qquad \int_a^b\ \to\ \int_{g(a)}^{g(b)}$$

The core intuition here is that substitution is the chain rule run backwards. Renaming the inner piece $u$ turns a tangled integral into a simple one.

*Example:* Find $\int_0^2 x\sqrt{x^2+5}\,dx$. Let $u=x^2+5$, so $x\,dx=\frac12du$, and the limits go from $5$ to $9$.
$$\tfrac12\int_5^9u^{1/2}du=\tfrac13\left(9^{3/2}-5^{3/2}\right)=\tfrac13(27-5\sqrt5)$$

*Trap:* Leaving an $x$ behind, or keeping the old limits.

*Check:* No $x$ may remain in the integral once you have switched to $u$.

name: Integration by parts
teach:
When the integrand is a product of unlike types, such as $x e^x$, $x\ln x$ or $x\cos x$, and substitution does not apply, choose $u$ by LIATE order: logarithm, inverse trig, algebraic, trig, exponential. Let $dv$ be the rest, and compute $du$ and $v$. If the new integral is not simpler, swap your choice. For a definite integral, put the limits on $uv$ as well.
$$\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du$$

The core intuition here is that integration by parts is the product rule run backwards. You trade a hard integral $\int u\,dv$ for another that should be easier.

*Example:* Find $\int x\sin x\,dx$. Let $u=x$ and $dv=\sin x\,dx$, so $du=dx$ and $v=-\cos x$.
$$-x\cos x+\int\cos x\,dx=-x\cos x+\sin x+C$$

*Trap:* Choosing $u$ so that the new integral is harder, or losing the minus sign in front of $\int v\,du$.

*Check:* Differentiate the result. The product rule should return $x\sin x$.

name: Trigonometric integrals
teach:
When the integrand is a product of powers of $\sin$ and $\cos$, or of $\tan$ and $\sec$, look at the powers. If a power is odd, save one factor, convert the rest with the Pythagorean identity, and substitute. If all powers are even, use the half-angle forms.
$$\sin^2x=\frac{1-\cos2x}{2},\qquad \cos^2x=\frac{1+\cos2x}{2},\qquad \sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$$

The core intuition here is that the Pythagorean identity trades one trig function for another, so an odd power can be reduced to a substitution. Even powers need double-angle identities.

*Example:* Find $\int\sin^2x\cos^3x\,dx$. Save one cosine and write $\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x$. Then let $u=\sin x$.
$$\int u^2(1-u^2)\,du=\frac{\sin^3x}{3}-\frac{\sin^5x}{5}+C$$

*Trap:* Using the half-angle form on an odd power, which makes the integral harder.

*Check:* Differentiate the result with the chain rule. You should recover the original product $\sin^2x\cos^3x$, which confirms the saved factor and the substitution were handled correctly.

name: Trigonometric substitution
teach:
When the integrand has a root such as $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$, $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$ or $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$ and ordinary substitution fails, choose the substitution by the pattern, then convert $dx$ as well. Simplify the root with the identity, integrate in $\theta$, and then draw a right triangle to turn the trig functions back into expressions in $x$. For a definite integral, change the limits to $\theta$ instead.
$$\sqrt{a^2-x^2}:\ x=a\sin\theta;\qquad \sqrt{a^2+x^2}:\ x=a\tan\theta;\qquad \sqrt{x^2-a^2}:\ x=a\sec\theta$$

The core intuition here is that each root matches a Pythagorean identity. The right substitution turns the root into a single trig function with no square root.

*Example:* Find $\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-25}}$ for $x>5$. Let $x=5\sec\theta$, so $dx=5\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta$ and $\sqrt{x^2-25}=5\tan\theta$.
$$\int\sec\theta\,d\theta=\ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|+C=\ln\left|\tfrac{x+\sqrt{x^2-25}}{5}\right|+C$$

*Trap:* Forgetting $dx$, or leaving the answer in $\theta$.

*Check:* The final result should be written in $x$ only, with no $\theta$ left. Differentiating it should give back the original integrand.

name: Partial fractions
teach:
When the integrand is a rational function $\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$ whose denominator factors, divide first if $\deg p\ge\deg q$. Then factor $q$ and write one term per factor. For a repeated factor use $\frac{A}{x-r}+\frac{B}{(x-r)^2}$, and for an irreducible quadratic use $\frac{Ax+B}{\cdots}$. Find the constants by cover-up or by comparing coefficients. For cover-up, hide the factor $x-r$ and evaluate the rest at $x=r$.
$$\frac{p}{(x-r)(x-s)}=\frac{A}{x-r}+\frac{B}{x-s}$$

The core intuition here is that a sum of simple fractions is easier to integrate than one complicated fraction. Partial fractions reverse the process of adding fractions with a common denominator.

*Example:* Find $\int\frac{3x+5}{(x+1)(x+3)}dx$. Cover-up gives $A=1$ at $x=-1$, and $B=2$ at $x=-3$.
$$\int\left(\frac{1}{x+1}+\frac{2}{x+3}\right)dx=\ln|x+1|+2\ln|x+3|+C$$

*Trap:* Skipping the polynomial division when the degrees are wrong.

*Check:* Recombine the fractions to confirm the numerator is $3x+5$.

name: Fundamental theorem of calculus
teach:
When a definite integral has a known antiderivative, or you must differentiate an integral whose limit contains $x$, use part 2 to evaluate integrals and part 1 to differentiate them. Here $F$ is any antiderivative of $f$. For part 1, put the top limit into $f$, then multiply by the derivative of that limit. If the lower limit also depends on $x$, subtract the same expression for it.
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a),\qquad \frac{d}{dx}\int_a^{h(x)}f(t)\,dt=f(h(x))\,h'(x)$$

The core intuition here is that integration accumulates a rate and differentiation reads off the rate. The two operations undo each other.

*Example:* Find $\frac{d}{dx}\int_1^{x^3}\sqrt{1+t^2}\,dt$.
$$\sqrt{1+x^6}\cdot3x^2$$

*Trap:* Subtracting in the wrong order, or forgetting the factor $h'(x)$.

*Check:* The integrand $f$ must be continuous on the whole interval for the theorem to apply.

name: Improper integrals
teach:
When an integral has an infinite limit, or its integrand blows up at an endpoint or inside the interval, replace the bad endpoint with a variable $t$, integrate, then take the limit. If the bad point is interior, split the integral there. The result either converges to a finite number or diverges. The $p$-test says $\int_1^\infty x^{-p}dx$ converges exactly when $p>1$, and $\int_0^1 x^{-p}dx$ converges exactly when $p<1$.
$$\int_a^\infty f=\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_a^tf$$

The core intuition here is that the ordinary definition needs a finite area over a bounded interval. A limit replaces the bad endpoint, and the answer is the value the area approaches, if it does.

*Example:* Evaluate $\int_0^1x^{-1/3}\,dx$, which blows up at $0$.
$$\lim_{t\to0^+}\left[\tfrac32x^{2/3}\right]_t^1=\tfrac32-0=\tfrac32$$

*Trap:* Applying the fundamental theorem across the bad point, or treating $\infty$ as a number.

*Check:* Here $p=\frac13<1$ near $0$, so the integral must converge, which matches the finite value.

name: Area and volume
teach:
When you need the area between curves, or the volume of a solid made by revolving a region about an axis, find the intersections first. For area, integrate top minus bottom. For revolution about the $x$-axis, use disks if the region touches the axis and washers if it leaves a gap, where $R$ is the outer radius and $r$ the inner radius. For revolution about the $y$-axis, shells of height $h$ at distance $x$ from the axis are often easier.
$$A=\int_a^b\big(f-g\big)\,dx,\qquad V=\pi\int_a^b\big(R^2-r^2\big)\,dx,\qquad V_{\text{shell}}=2\pi\int_a^b x\,h\,dx$$

The core intuition here is that both are integrals of slices. Area uses thin strips, and volume stacks thin disks, washers or shells.

*Example:* Revolve the region under $y=x^2$ on $[0,2]$ about the $x$-axis.
$$V=\pi\int_0^2x^4\,dx=\pi\cdot\tfrac{32}{5}=\tfrac{32\pi}{5}$$

*Trap:* Using the wrong radius, or squaring the difference $R-r$ instead of $R^2-r^2$.

*Check:* The volume must be positive, and a sketch should show which curve is outer.

name: Arc length, surface area, averages
teach:
When you need the length of a curve, the area of a surface of revolution, or the mean value of a function, use these formulas for $y=f(x)$ on $[a,b]$. The surface formula is for revolution about the $x$-axis. Square $f'$ first, then simplify under the root, where it is often a perfect square.
$$L=\int_a^b\sqrt{1+(f')^2}\,dx,\qquad S=2\pi\int_a^bf\sqrt{1+(f')^2}\,dx,\qquad f_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^bf\,dx$$

The core intuition here is that a tiny piece of curve has length $\sqrt{dx^2+dy^2}$, which gives the arc length formula. The average of a function is its area divided by the width.

*Example:* Find the average of $f(x)=x^2+1$ on $[0,3]$.
$$\frac13\int_0^3(x^2+1)\,dx=\frac13\left(9+3\right)=4$$

*Trap:* Forgetting to square $f'$, dropping the $2\pi$, or leaving out the factor $\frac{1}{b-a}$.

*Check:* The average must lie between the minimum and maximum of $f$ on the interval.

name: Sequence limits
teach:
When you want the limit of a sequence $a_n$ as $n\to\infty$, divide top and bottom of a ratio of polynomials by the highest power of $n$. Compare growth rates, since logarithms are slower than powers, powers are slower than exponentials, and exponentials are slower than factorials. Use the squeeze theorem when the terms are bounded between two known sequences.
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}r^n=0\ (|r|<1),\qquad \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\frac xn\right)^n=e^x$$

The core intuition here is that only the fastest-growing part of a formula matters for large $n$. Dividing by it reveals the limit.

*Example:* Find $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{5n^3-n}{2n^3+7n^2}$.
$$\frac{5-\frac1{n^2}}{2+\frac7n}\;\longrightarrow\;\frac52$$

*Trap:* Stopping at an indeterminate form like $\frac\infty\infty$ without dividing out the growth.

*Check:* Equal degrees on top and bottom give the ratio of the leading coefficients, and a lower degree on top gives $0$.

name: Series convergence tests
teach:
When you must decide whether an infinite sum $\sum a_n$ converges, check the terms first, then pick a test. Use comparison or limit comparison against the benchmark series below. Use the ratio test for factorials and powers: with $L=\lim\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|$, the series converges if $L<1$ and diverges if $L>1$. Use the integral test for a positive decreasing $f$.
$$a_n\not\to0\Rightarrow\text{diverges};\qquad \sum\frac1{n^p}\ \text{converges}\iff p>1;\qquad \sum r^n\ \text{converges}\iff|r|<1$$

The core intuition here is that a series converges only if its partial sums settle. If the terms do not shrink to zero, the sum cannot settle, so a quick test can rule many series out.

*Example:* Does $\sum\frac{3n+1}{n^4+5}$ converge? Compare with $\sum\frac1{n^3}$. The limit is positive and finite, and $p=3>1$, so it converges.
$$\lim\frac{(3n+1)/(n^4+5)}{1/n^3}=\lim\frac{3n^4+n^3}{n^4+5}=3$$

*Trap:* Concluding convergence from $a_n\to0$ alone. The series $\sum\frac1n$ diverges.

*Check:* Name the test you used and confirm its conditions hold.

name: Alternating and conditional convergence
teach:
When the terms of a series alternate in sign, such as $\sum(-1)^n a_n$ with $a_n>0$, apply the alternating series test. The series converges if $a_n$ decreases and $a_n\to0$, and after $N$ terms the error is at most the first omitted term. Then test $\sum|a_n|$. If it converges, the series converges absolutely, and if not, it converges only conditionally.
$$\left|S-S_N\right|\le a_{N+1}$$

The core intuition here is that alternating terms overshoot and undershoot. So the partial sums trap the total between consecutive values, which also bounds the error.

*Example:* Does $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(-1)^n}{\sqrt n}$ converge, and how? The terms decrease to $0$, but $\sum\frac1{\sqrt n}$ diverges with $p=\frac12$, so it converges conditionally.
$$\tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\ \text{decreases to }0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{converges};\quad \sum\tfrac1{\sqrt n}\ \text{diverges}\ (p=\tfrac12)$$

*Trap:* Claiming absolute convergence when only the alternating test was checked.

*Check:* The error is no larger than the first omitted term, and it has the sign of that term.

name: Power series
teach:
When a series has the form $\sum c_n(x-a)^n$ and you need the values of $x$ where it converges, compute the limit $L$ below and set the radius of convergence $R=\frac1L$. The series converges for $|x-a|<R$. If $L=0$ then $R=\infty$ and it converges for every $x$, and if $L=\infty$ then $R=0$ and it converges only at the center. Then test each endpoint on its own with a number-series test. The geometric series is $\sum x^n=\frac{1}{1-x}$ for $|x|<1$.
$$L=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{c_{n+1}}{c_n}\right|,\qquad R=\frac1L,\qquad |x-a|<R$$

The core intuition here is that for a fixed $x$ the series is an ordinary series. It converges inside a symmetric interval around $a$ and diverges outside it, and the ratio test finds the interval.

*Example:* Find the interval for $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(x+1)^n}{2^n n^2}$, whose center is $-1$. Here $L=\frac12$, so $R=2$. Both endpoints converge, so the interval is $[-3,1]$.
$$-3<x<1;\quad x=1:\ \sum\tfrac1{n^2}\ \text{converges};\quad x=-3:\ \sum\tfrac{(-1)^n}{n^2}\ \text{converges}$$

*Trap:* Stopping at the open interval and forgetting the endpoints. The ratio test says nothing there, so each endpoint needs its own test.

*Check:* The interval must be centered at $a$, apart from the endpoints you included or excluded.

name: Taylor series
teach:
When you want a function as a power series about a point, or a polynomial approximation near it, use the fact that the coefficient of $(x-a)^n$ is $\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}$. Memorize the series about $0$ below, then substitute into them or integrate them term by term to get new ones.
$$e^x=\sum\frac{x^n}{n!},\qquad \sin x=\sum\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad \cos x=\sum\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}$$
$$\frac{1}{1-x}=\sum x^n\ (|x|<1),\qquad \ln(1+x)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}x^n}{n}\ (|x|<1)$$

The core intuition here is that a smooth function is matched near $a$ by a polynomial whose derivatives at $a$ equal its own. The first term fits the value, the next fits the slope, and each added term gives a closer fit.

*Example:* Find the first three nonzero terms of $e^{-x^2}$ by putting $-x^2$ into the series for $e^x$.
$$e^{-x^2}=1-x^2+\frac{x^4}{2}-\cdots$$

*Trap:* Dropping the factorial, or the alternating signs in the sine and cosine series.

*Check:* At $x=0$ the series must equal $f(0)$. Here the series gives $1$ and $e^{0}=1$, so the constant term is right.

name: Parametric and polar curves
teach:
When a curve is given by $x(t),y(t)$ or in polar form $r(\theta)$, evaluate both rates at the given $t$, then divide to get the slope. Convert polar to rectangular with $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$. For polar area, choose the $\theta$ range that traces the curve once.
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt},\qquad L=\int\sqrt{(x')^2+(y')^2}\,dt,\qquad A=\frac12\int r^2\,d\theta$$

The core intuition here is that a parametric curve traces a path as the parameter $t$ runs, and its slope is the ratio of the vertical rate to the horizontal rate. Polar area adds thin pie-slice sectors, each with area $\frac12r^2\,d\theta$.

*Example:* Find the slope of $x=t^3-t$, $y=t^2$ at $t=2$.
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2t}{3t^2-1}=\frac{4}{11}$$

*Trap:* Inverting the slope to $\frac{dx/dt}{dy/dt}$, or dropping the $\frac12$ in polar area.

*Check:* If $\frac{dx}{dt}=0$ while $\frac{dy}{dt}\ne0$, the tangent is vertical and the slope is undefined.

name: Vector operations
teach:
When a problem asks for a dot product, cross product, length, angle or projection of vectors in $\mathbb R^3$, work from the components of $\mathbf u=\langle u_1,u_2,u_3\rangle$ and $\mathbf v=\langle v_1,v_2,v_3\rangle$. The dot product is zero for perpendicular vectors, and the cross product is zero for parallel vectors. The length is $\|\mathbf u\|=\sqrt{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}$, and the projection of $\mathbf u$ on $\mathbf v$ is $\frac{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v}{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf v}\mathbf v$. Here $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors, and you can compute the cross product from the components or as a $3\times3$ determinant.
$$\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=u_1v_1+u_2v_2+u_3v_3=\|\mathbf u\|\|\mathbf v\|\cos\theta,\qquad \|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\|=\|\mathbf u\|\|\mathbf v\|\sin\theta$$
$$\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\langle u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\ u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\ u_1v_2-u_2v_1\rangle$$

The core intuition here is that the dot product measures how much two vectors point the same way, and it is a number. The cross product gives a new vector perpendicular to both, whose length is the area of their parallelogram.

*Example:* Find $\langle2,0,1\rangle\times\langle1,3,0\rangle$.
$$\langle 0\cdot0-1\cdot3,\ 1\cdot1-2\cdot0,\ 2\cdot3-0\cdot1\rangle=\langle-3,1,6\rangle$$

*Trap:* Swapping the order flips the sign, because $\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=-\,\mathbf v\times\mathbf u$.

*Check:* The dot product of the result with each input vector must be zero.

name: Lines and planes in R3
teach:
When you must write a line or plane in $\mathbb R^3$, find where they meet, or find a distance, start from a point $P_0$, a direction $\mathbf d$ for a line, and a normal $\mathbf n=\langle a,b,c\rangle$ for a plane. The direction through two points $P$ and $Q$ is $Q-P$. A plane through three points has a normal equal to the cross product of two edge vectors. To intersect a line with a plane, substitute the line into the plane and solve for $t$. The distance from $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ to the plane $ax+by+cz=d$ is $\frac{|ax_1+by_1+cz_1-d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$.
$$\mathbf r(t)=P_0+t\,\mathbf d,\qquad a(x-x_0)+b(y-y_0)+c(z-z_0)=0$$

The core intuition here is that a line needs a point and a direction. A plane needs a point and a normal vector, which is perpendicular to every direction lying in the plane.

*Example:* Find where $(1+t,\ 2t,\ 3-t)$ meets the plane $x+2y+z=12$.
$$(1+t)+4t+(3-t)=12\;\Longrightarrow\;4t=8\;\Longrightarrow\;t=2,\quad \text{point }(3,4,1)$$

*Trap:* Mixing up the plane's constant with its normal, or a point with a direction.

*Check:* The intersection point satisfies the plane equation.

name: Partial derivatives
teach:
When a function has several inputs and you ask how it changes when one input moves and the others stay fixed, treat every other variable as a constant and differentiate in the one you want. Mixed partials of smooth functions agree, so $f_{xy}=f_{yx}$. Use the chain and product rules as usual.
$$f_x=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h,y)-f(x,y)}{h}$$

The core intuition here is that freezing the other variables turns a many-variable function into an ordinary one-variable function, so the usual rules apply.

*Example:* For $f(x,y)=x^2y+e^{xy}$, find $f_x$ and $f_y$.
$$f_x=2xy+y\,e^{xy},\qquad f_y=x^2+x\,e^{xy}$$

*Trap:* Differentiating a term in $y$ when you are working in $x$. A factor with only $y$ in it is a constant and stays.

*Check:* Take $f_{xy}$ and $f_{yx}$. They should match.

name: Multivariable chain rule
teach:
When $z=f(x,y)$ and the inputs $x$ and $y$ themselves depend on another variable, such as $t$, or on two others, draw the tree from $z$ down to $t$ and sum over every path. Multiply along each path. With a third input, add a third term. With two parameters, use $\frac{\partial z}{\partial s}=f_x x_s+f_y y_s$. Evaluate the partials at the point and the derivatives at the same parameter value.
$$\frac{dz}{dt}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dt}$$

The core intuition here is that a change in $t$ moves $z$ along every path that leads there. Each path contributes a rate, and you add them.

*Example:* Let $z=x^2y$ with $x=t^2$ and $y=3t$, and find $\frac{dz}{dt}$.
$$2xy\cdot2t+x^2\cdot3=2(t^2)(3t)(2t)+t^4\cdot3=12t^4+3t^4=15t^4$$

*Trap:* Dropping one of the terms, or using $x$ where the derivative $x'$ is needed.

*Check:* Substitute first. Here $z=3t^5$, so $\frac{dz}{dt}=15t^4$, which agrees.

name: Gradient and directional derivative
teach:
When you need the rate of change of $f$ in a particular direction, or the direction of steepest increase, compute $\nabla f$, normalize the direction, then take a dot product. The gradient points uphill, is perpendicular to level curves, and its length is the greatest rate of change.
$$\nabla f=\langle f_x,f_y\rangle,\qquad D_{\mathbf u}f=\nabla f\cdot\mathbf u,\quad \|\mathbf u\|=1$$

The core intuition here is that the gradient collects all the partials into one vector. Its dot product with a direction measures the slope that way, and it is largest when the direction matches the gradient.

*Example:* Take $f=xy+y^2$ at $(2,1)$ in the direction $\langle5,12\rangle$.
$$\nabla f=\langle y,\ x+2y\rangle=\langle1,4\rangle,\quad \mathbf u=\tfrac1{13}\langle5,12\rangle,\quad D_{\mathbf u}f=\tfrac{5+48}{13}=\tfrac{53}{13}$$

*Trap:* Forgetting to divide the direction by its length when it is not a unit vector.

*Check:* The result cannot exceed $\|\nabla f\|=\sqrt{17}\approx4.12$. Here $\frac{53}{13}\approx4.08$ passes.

name: Multivariable extrema
teach:
When you need to find and classify the local maxima, minima and saddle points of $f(x,y)$, solve $f_x=0$ and $f_y=0$ for the critical points. At each one, compute the discriminant $D$ below. If $D>0$ and $f_{xx}>0$ it is a local minimum, and if $D>0$ and $f_{xx}<0$ it is a local maximum. If $D<0$ it is a saddle, and if $D=0$ the test fails. On a closed region, also evaluate $f$ on each boundary piece and at the corners, then compare every value.
$$D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2$$

The core intuition here is that at a smooth extremum the surface is flat in every direction, so both partials vanish. The second derivatives then tell you whether the surface curves up, down, or both ways.

*Example:* Classify the critical point of $f=x^2+xy+y^2-3x$. The partials give the point $(2,-1)$, and $D>0$ with $f_{xx}>0$ makes it a local minimum.
$$f_x=2x+y-3=0,\ f_y=x+2y=0\ \Rightarrow\ (2,-1),\quad D=2\cdot2-1=3>0,\ f_{xx}=2>0$$

*Trap:* On a closed region, the boundary can hold extrema that are not critical points.

*Check:* Verify that both partials vanish at the point you found.

name: Lagrange multipliers
teach:
When you must maximize or minimize $f$ while a constraint $g=c$ holds, solve the gradient condition together with the constraint. The number $\lambda$ is the multiplier. Write one equation per component, eliminate $\lambda$, and substitute into the constraint. Evaluate $f$ at every candidate and compare. On a closed bounded constraint set, the largest and smallest values are the extremes.
$$\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g,\qquad g(x,y)=c$$

The core intuition here is that at the best point on the constraint curve, a level curve of $f$ just touches it. So the gradients of $f$ and $g$ point along the same line.

*Example:* Minimize $x^2+2y^2$ subject to $x+y=3$.
$$2x=\lambda,\ 4y=\lambda\ \Rightarrow\ x=2y,\quad 3y=3\ \Rightarrow\ y=1,\ x=2,\ f=6$$

*Trap:* Dropping the constraint equation, which leaves too many solutions.

*Check:* The candidate must satisfy $g=c$.

name: Double integrals
teach:
When you integrate over a flat region, for area, mass, volume under a surface or an average value, sketch the region and write its bounds. Then integrate the inner variable, treating the outer one as a constant. Swapping the order changes the bounds, so redraw the region first.
$$\iint_Rf\,dA=\int_a^b\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx$$

The core intuition here is that you slice the region into thin strips, integrate each strip, then add up the strips. The two integrations are done one at a time, inner first.

*Example:* Integrate $f=x+y$ over the triangle with $0\le y\le x\le 2$.
$$\int_0^2\int_0^x(x+y)\,dy\,dx=\int_0^2\left(x^2+\tfrac{x^2}{2}\right)dx=\int_0^2\tfrac{3x^2}{2}dx=4$$

*Trap:* Swapping the order of integration without redrawing the region.

*Check:* The inner integral should leave a function of the outer variable only.

name: Polar, cylindrical, spherical integrals
teach:
When a region or integrand is round, such as a disk, cone, sphere or cylinder, or involves $x^2+y^2$, substitute, convert the bounds, and include the Jacobian factor. Use $x^2+y^2=r^2$ and $x^2+y^2+z^2=\rho^2$. In spherical coordinates, $\phi$ is the angle from the positive $z$-axis.
$$dA=r\,dr\,d\theta,\qquad dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz,\qquad dV=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$$

The core intuition here is that in polar coordinates tiny cells are not rectangles of area $dx\,dy$. A cell at radius $r$ has width $dr$ and arc length $r\,d\theta$, so an extra factor of $r$ appears, and spherical cells stretch in two directions, so they gain two factors.

*Example:* Integrate $x^2+y^2$ over the disk of radius $2$.
$$\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2 r^2\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta=2\pi\cdot\frac{2^4}{4}=8\pi$$

*Trap:* Omitting the factor $r$ or $\rho^2\sin\phi$, which is the most common error in these integrals.

*Check:* With integrand $1$, you should recover the area or volume you already know, such as $\pi r^2$ for a disk.

name: Triple integrals
teach:
When you need a volume, mass or average over a solid region in $\mathbb R^3$, sketch the solid and project it onto a plane, then write bounds from the inside out. An inner bound may use outer variables only. For a box, any order works, and for a round solid, switch to cylindrical or spherical coordinates.
$$\iiint_Ef\,dV=\int_a^b\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)}\int_{h_1(x,y)}^{h_2(x,y)}f\,dz\,dy\,dx$$

The core intuition here is that you add up a function over tiny boxes by integrating one variable at a time. Each integral reduces the dimension by one.

*Example:* The volume of the solid under $z=x+y$ above the square $[0,1]^2$ is:
$$\int_0^1\int_0^1\int_0^{x+y}dz\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1\int_0^1(x+y)\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1\left(x+\tfrac12\right)dx=1$$

*Trap:* An inner bound that uses a variable not yet fixed by an outer integral.

*Check:* With integrand $1$ the result should be positive and equal the volume.

name: Line integrals and conservative fields
teach:
When you integrate a vector field $\mathbf F$ along a curve $C$ to find work or circulation, parametrize $C$ as $\mathbf r(t)$ for $a\le t\le b$. For $\int_CP\,dx+Q\,dy$, put $x=x(t)$, $y=y(t)$ and $dx=x'\,dt$, $dy=y'\,dt$. If $\mathbf F=\nabla\varphi$, the result is $\varphi(B)-\varphi(A)$. On a simply connected region, $\mathbf F=\langle P,Q\rangle$ is conservative when $Q_x=P_y$.
$$\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_a^b\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)\,dt$$

The core intuition here is that the integral adds up the part of the field that points along each tiny step of the path. If the field is a gradient, the answer depends only on the endpoints, so the shape of the path does not matter and you can choose the easiest one.

*Example:* For $\mathbf F=\langle y^2,2xy\rangle$ from $(0,0)$ to $(2,3)$, take $\varphi=xy^2$ since $\nabla\varphi=\langle y^2,2xy\rangle$.
$$\varphi(2,3)-\varphi(0,0)=18$$

*Trap:* Using $\varphi(A)-\varphi(B)$ with the endpoints reversed.

*Check:* A closed loop in a conservative field must give zero, since the start and end points coincide.

name: Green's theorem
teach:
When a line integral $\oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy$ goes around a closed curve and the region inside is easier to handle, check that $C$ is simple, closed and positively oriented, meaning counterclockwise, and that $P$ and $Q$ are smooth inside. Then compute the integrand first and integrate over the region $D$. With $P=-y$ and $Q=x$, the area of $D$ is $\frac12\oint x\,dy-y\,dx$.
$$\oint_CP\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dA$$

The core intuition here is that the circulation around the boundary equals the total tiny spin inside. Interior contributions cancel, leaving only the boundary.

*Example:* Let $P=xy$ and $Q=0$, counterclockwise around the rectangle $[0,2]\times[0,1]$.
$$Q_x-P_y=-x,\qquad \int_0^1\int_0^2(-x)\,dx\,dy=-2$$

*Trap:* Reversing the sign of $Q_x-P_y$, or applying it to an open curve.

*Check:* Compute the line integral directly. Only the top edge contributes, since $y=0$ on the bottom and $dx=0$ on the sides. It runs from $x=2$ to $x=0$ at $y=1$, and gives $\int_2^0x\,dx=-2$.

name: Divergence, curl, surface integrals
teach:
When you need the divergence or curl of a vector field, or must use their identities, work from the components of $\mathbf F=\langle P,Q,R\rangle$. Divergence is a number and curl is a vector. Two identities hold for smooth fields: $\nabla\times(\nabla\varphi)=\mathbf 0$ and $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf F)=0$.
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=P_x+Q_y+R_z,\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf F=\langle R_y-Q_z,\ P_z-R_x,\ Q_x-P_y\rangle$$

The core intuition here is that divergence measures how much the field spreads out from a point, like a source. Curl measures how much it spins around the point, like a whirlpool. Both are built from partial derivatives.

*Example:* Let $\mathbf F=\langle x^2y,\ yz,\ xz\rangle$, so $P=x^2y$, $Q=yz$ and $R=xz$.
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=2xy+z+x,\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf F=\langle0-y,\ 0-z,\ 0-x^2\rangle=\langle-y,\,-z,\,-x^2\rangle$$

*Trap:* Mixing up the signs or the order of the curl components.

*Check:* The divergence of a curl must vanish. Here $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(-y)+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(-z)+\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(-x^2)=0$.

name: Stokes and divergence theorems
teach:
When you want the circulation around a curve that bounds a surface, or the flux of a field through a closed surface, choose the theorem by the shape. Stokes applies when a curve $C$ bounds a surface $S$ with matching orientation. The divergence theorem applies when a closed surface $S$ bounds a solid $E$, with the normal pointing outward. For a flat region in the $xy$-plane with $C$ counterclockwise, the normal is $+\mathbf k$ and the integrand is $Q_x-P_y$.
$$\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot d\mathbf S,\qquad \oiint_S\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S=\iiint_E\nabla\cdot\mathbf F\,dV$$

The core intuition here is that both theorems turn a hard integral into an easier one of one dimension higher or lower. Local spin or spread inside adds up to what happens on the boundary.

*Example:* Find the outward flux of $\mathbf F=\langle x,y,z\rangle$ through the sphere of radius $2$.
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=3,\qquad \text{flux}=3\cdot\tfrac43\pi(2)^3=32\pi$$

*Trap:* Applying Stokes to a closed surface, which has no boundary curve, or using an inward normal.

*Check:* On the sphere, $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n=2$ everywhere and the area is $16\pi$, so the flux is $32\pi$ directly.

name: Matrix algebra
teach:
When a problem asks for a product, sum, transpose or trace of matrices, or for the size of a result, first check that the inner sizes match. An $m\times n$ matrix times an $n\times p$ matrix is $m\times p$. Then dot row $i$ of $A$ with column $j$ of $B$ to get entry $(i,j)$. For the transpose of a product, reverse the order. The trace is the sum of the diagonal entries, and $\operatorname{tr}(cA)=c\operatorname{tr}A$.
$$(AB)_{ij}=\sum_k A_{ik}B_{kj},\qquad (AB)^T=B^TA^T$$

The core intuition here is that matrix multiplication pairs rows of the left factor with columns of the right factor. That pairing fixes both the size rule and the failure of commutativity.

*Example:* Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&0\end{pmatrix}$. Each entry is a row-column dot product, so the top-left entry of $AB$ is $1\cdot4+2\cdot2=8$. Swapping the order gives a different matrix.
$$AB=\begin{pmatrix}8&1\\6&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad BA=\begin{pmatrix}4&11\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$$

*Trap:* Do not assume $AB=BA$, since the example shows they differ. Also reverse the order in $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$ rather than writing $A^TB^T$.

*Check:* The result has the row count of the left factor and the column count of the right factor.

name: Row reduction
teach:
When a linear system must be solved, or a rank, pivot count or echelon form is asked for, work column by column with the three allowed operations: swapping two rows, scaling a row by a nonzero number, and adding a multiple of one row to another. Pick a pivot, then clear every entry below it. For a system, reduce the augmented matrix and read the answers from the bottom row up. The rank is the number of nonzero rows left.
$$R_i\to R_i-c\,R_j$$

The core intuition here is that these three row operations never change the solution set. They turn a tangled system into a staircase that can be read off from the bottom up.

*Example:* Reduce the matrix below. There are two pivots, so the rank is $2$.
$$\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\2&5&3\\1&3&2\end{pmatrix}\xrightarrow{R_2-2R_1,\;R_3-R_1}\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\0&1&1\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}\xrightarrow{R_3-R_2}\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$$

*Trap:* Scaling a row by $0$ destroys an equation. A row reading $0=5$ means the system has no solution.

*Check:* In the original matrix, row $2$ minus row $1$ equals row $3$. One row depends on the others, so rank $2$ is right.

name: Determinants
teach:
When a square $n\times n$ matrix needs an invertibility test, a volume factor, or a product or power of determinants, use the $2\times2$ formula directly. For larger sizes, row-reduce to triangular form and multiply the diagonal. Each row swap flips the sign, and adding a multiple of one row to another changes nothing.
$$\det\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}=ad-bc,\qquad \det(AB)=\det A\,\det B,\qquad \det(cA)=c^n\det A$$

The core intuition here is that the determinant is the signed volume scale of the map. It is zero exactly when the map flattens space, so the matrix is not invertible.

*Example:* Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\3&5&2\\1&0&4\end{pmatrix}$. Subtract $3R_1$ from $R_2$ and $R_1$ from $R_3$, then subtract $2R_2$ from $R_3$. The diagonal becomes $1,-1,5$, so
$$\det A=-5,\qquad \det(3A)=3^3(-5)=-135$$

*Trap:* Writing $\det(cA)=c\det A$. Every one of the $n$ rows picks up the factor $c$.

*Check:* A zero determinant must match dependent rows or columns.

name: Matrix inverse
teach:
When a system $A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ must be solved by inverting, or $A^{-1}$ or a product of inverses is needed, compute $ad-bc$ first. If it is zero, stop, because no inverse exists. Otherwise swap the two diagonal entries, negate the other two, and divide everything by the determinant. For larger matrices, row-reduce the block matrix $[A\mid I]$ until the left half is $I$. The right half is then $A^{-1}$.
$$\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}^{-1}=\frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix},\qquad (AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$$

The core intuition here is that the inverse undoes $A$. It exists only when $A$ does not collapse any direction, which means $\det A\neq0$.

*Example:* Invert $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\5&2\end{pmatrix}$. The determinant is $6-5=1$, so no division is needed. Swap $3$ and $2$, then negate $1$ and $5$.
$$A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-5&3\end{pmatrix}$$

*Trap:* Forgetting the minus signs on $b$ and $c$, or the factor $\frac1{\det}$.

*Check:* Multiply $AA^{-1}$ and look for $I$.

name: Vector spaces and subspaces
teach:
When a set of vectors, polynomials or matrices is claimed to be a subspace, or a solution set is described, test the zero vector first, since a failure there ends the question. Then check closure for general $\mathbf u,\mathbf v$ and every scalar $c$. Sets cut out by $A\mathbf x=\mathbf 0$ always pass.
$$\mathbf 0\in W,\qquad \mathbf u,\mathbf v\in W\Rightarrow \mathbf u+\mathbf v\in W,\qquad c\mathbf u\in W$$

The core intuition here is that a subspace is a set that stays inside itself under the two basic operations. Anything that can be built from its members by adding and scaling must also be a member.

*Example:* Is $W=\{(x,y,z): x=2z\}$ a subspace of $\mathbb R^3$? The zero vector fits. Take two members and add them. Scaling works the same way, so $W$ is a subspace.
$$(2z_1,y_1,z_1)+(2z_2,y_2,z_2)=(2(z_1+z_2),\,y_1+y_2,\,z_1+z_2)\in W$$

*Trap:* Testing one pair of numbers. Closure must hold for all members.

*Check:* A set with a constant term like $x+y=1$ misses $\mathbf 0$.

name: Span, independence, basis, dimension
teach:
When a question asks about span, independence, a basis, or the dimension of a space or subspace, put the vectors as columns of a matrix and row-reduce. The pivot columns are independent, and their count is the dimension of the span. In $\mathbb R^n$, more than $n$ vectors are always dependent, and fewer than $n$ never span.
$$c_1\mathbf v_1+\cdots+c_k\mathbf v_k=\mathbf 0\;\Rightarrow\;\text{all }c_i=0\quad(\text{independent})$$

The core intuition here is that a basis is the smallest set that still reaches everything. Its size is the same for every basis, so it measures the space.

*Example:* Find the dimension of the span of $(1,0,3)$, $(0,1,2)$, $(1,1,5)$. The third is the sum of the first two, so it adds nothing. There are two pivots, so the dimension is $2$.
$$\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\3&2&5\end{pmatrix}\to\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\0&2&2\end{pmatrix}\to\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$$

*Trap:* Counting the vectors given instead of the pivots.

*Check:* The dimension cannot exceed the number of vectors or the ambient size.

name: Rank-nullity
teach:
When a matrix or linear map has its rank, kernel, image or nullity asked for, and you know all but one of them, use the formula below. Here $V$ is the domain and $T$ the map. For an $m\times n$ matrix the domain is $\mathbb R^n$, so $n$ is the column count. The rank is the dimension of the image, which is also the number of pivots and the dimension of the column space. Subtract the known part from $n$.
$$\operatorname{rank}T+\dim\ker T=\dim V$$

The core intuition here is that each input direction either survives into the image or is crushed into the kernel. Together they use up the whole domain.

*Example:* A matrix has $9$ columns and $6$ rows, and its rank is $6$. The nullity comes from the column count, and the image has dimension $6$ inside $\mathbb R^6$, so it fills the target.
$$\dim\ker=9-6=3$$

*Trap:* Subtracting from the row count. The rows give the size of the target, not the domain.

*Check:* The rank is at most the smaller of the row and column counts.

name: Linear transformations
teach:
When a map $T$ is given by a rule and you must test linearity, build its matrix, or find its kernel or image, first check the two rules below. A constant term breaks them. To build the matrix, apply $T$ to each standard basis vector $e_i$ and write the results as columns. The kernel is the set of $\mathbf x$ with $T\mathbf x=\mathbf 0$.
