$$T(\mathbf u+\mathbf v)=T\mathbf u+T\mathbf v,\qquad T(c\mathbf u)=cT\mathbf u,\qquad [T]=\big(T(e_1)\;\cdots\;T(e_n)\big)$$

The core intuition here is that a linear map is fixed by what it does to the basis vectors. Knowing $T(e_1),\dots,T(e_n)$ gives the whole map.

*Example:* Let $T(x,y,z)=(x-z,\;2y+z)$ and apply it to $e_1$, $e_2$, $e_3$ in turn.
$$[T]=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&-1\\0&2&1\end{pmatrix}$$

*Trap:* Writing the results as rows instead of columns, or calling $T(x,y)=(x+3,y)$ linear when $T(\mathbf 0)\neq\mathbf 0$.

*Check:* The matrix has one column per input coordinate.

name: Change of basis and similarity
teach:
When a vector or map must be written in a new basis $\mathcal B$, or two matrices are claimed to represent the same map, let $P$ have the new basis vectors as columns. Then $P$ turns new coordinates $[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}$ into standard ones. To get new coordinates from standard ones, solve $P\mathbf c=\mathbf x$. Similar matrices share trace, determinant and eigenvalues.
$$\mathbf x=P\,[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B},\qquad B=P^{-1}AP$$

The core intuition here is that the map does not change, only the coordinates do. The matrix $P$ translates between the two coordinate systems.

*Example:* Take the basis $\mathbf b_1=(1,2)$ and $\mathbf b_2=(0,1)$ and find the coordinates of $\mathbf x=(3,7)$. The coordinates are $(3,1)$.
$$c_1(1,2)+c_2(0,1)=(3,7)\Rightarrow c_1=3,\;c_2=1$$

*Trap:* Using $P^T$, or writing $PAP^{-1}$ in the wrong order. The inverse goes on the left of $A$.

*Check:* Multiply $P[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}$ and recover $\mathbf x$.

name: Eigenvalues of small matrices
teach:
When a $2\times2$ matrix needs eigenvalues, or its trace and determinant are linked to them, compute the trace, the sum of the diagonal entries, and the determinant. Write the quadratic below and solve it. The roots add to the trace and multiply to the determinant, so $\lambda_1^2+\lambda_2^2=(\operatorname{tr}A)^2-2\det A$.
$$\lambda^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)\,\lambda+\det A=0$$

The core intuition here is that an eigenvector is only stretched by $A$. That happens exactly when $A-\lambda I$ is singular, so its determinant vanishes.

*Example:* Take $A=\begin{pmatrix}5&1\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$, with trace $9$ and determinant $20-2=18$. The eigenvalues are $3$ and $6$.
$$\lambda^2-9\lambda+18=(\lambda-3)(\lambda-6)=0$$

*Trap:* Using $+\operatorname{tr}A$ in the middle term, or a wrong sign on the determinant term.

*Check:* Subtract the eigenvalue from the diagonal and confirm the determinant is zero. For $\lambda=3$ this gives $2\cdot1-1\cdot2=0$.

name: Diagonalization
teach:
When a power $A^k$ is wanted, or you must decide whether $A=PDP^{-1}$ exists, find the eigenvalues, then each eigenspace by solving $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$. Here $D$ holds the eigenvalues and $P$ holds matching eigenvectors as columns. Also $\operatorname{tr}A^k=\sum\lambda_i^k$ and $\det A^k=\prod\lambda_i^k$. The matrix diagonalizes exactly when the eigenvectors fill a basis, and distinct eigenvalues always suffice.
$$A=PDP^{-1}\;\Rightarrow\;A^k=PD^kP^{-1}$$

The core intuition here is that in an eigenbasis the matrix just scales each axis, so powers become powers of the scalars.

*Example:* A $2\times2$ matrix $A$ has eigenvalues $1$ and $-2$. Then $\operatorname{tr}(A^4)$ and $\det(A^4)$ follow without finding $P$.
$$\operatorname{tr}(A^4)=1^4+(-2)^4=17,\qquad \det(A^4)=(-2)^4=16$$

*Trap:* Assuming every matrix diagonalizes. A repeated eigenvalue with a one-dimensional eigenspace fails.

*Check:* The product of the diagonal entries of $D$ must equal $\det A$.

name: Cayley-Hamilton and minimal polynomial
teach:
When a high power of a small matrix, or its inverse, is needed without diagonalizing, use the $2\times2$ case below. Solve it for $A^2$ in terms of $A$ and $I$. Multiply by $A$ again to reduce $A^3$, and repeat for higher powers. To get the inverse, move the $I$ term alone to one side, then factor $A$ out of the other side.
$$A^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)A+(\det A)I=0$$

The core intuition here is that a matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial. That lets you rewrite any higher power in terms of lower ones.

*Example:* Let $\operatorname{tr}A=4$ and $\det A=1$, so $A^2=4A-I$. Then the cube follows.
$$A^3=4A^2-A=4(4A-I)-A=15A-4I$$

*Trap:* Dropping the determinant term, or substituting the scalar $\det A$ where $\det A\,I$ belongs.

*Check:* Take traces of $A^3=15A-4I$, which gives $15\cdot4-4\cdot2=52$. This equals $\lambda_1^3+\lambda_2^3=4^3-3\cdot1\cdot4$.

name: Inner products and Gram-Schmidt
teach:
When lengths, angles, orthogonality or projections appear, or an orthogonal basis must be built, use the projection formula below. Here $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\sum u_iv_i$ and the length is $\|\mathbf v\|=\sqrt{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf v}$. Vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is $0$. For Gram-Schmidt, keep $\mathbf u_1=\mathbf v_1$. Then subtract from each later vector its projections onto the earlier ones, and divide by the length at the end if unit vectors are wanted.
$$\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf u}\mathbf v=\frac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}\,\mathbf u$$

The core intuition here is that the dot product measures how much two vectors point the same way. Removing that shared part leaves a perpendicular piece.

*Example:* Take $\mathbf v_1=(1,2)$ and $\mathbf v_2=(3,1)$, and subtract the projection of $\mathbf v_2$ onto $\mathbf v_1$.
$$\mathbf u_2=(3,1)-\frac{5}{5}(1,2)=(2,-1)$$

*Trap:* Dividing by $\|\mathbf u\|$ instead of $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u$ in the projection formula.

*Check:* The leftover vector must have dot product $0$ with the one removed. Here $(1,2)\cdot(2,-1)=0$.

name: Symmetric matrices and quadratic forms
teach:
When a real symmetric matrix or a quadratic form $\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x$ is given, and its extreme values or definiteness matter, find the eigenvalues, which are always real. On the unit sphere the form runs from the smallest to the largest eigenvalue. All $\lambda_i>0$ means positive definite.
$$A=QDQ^T,\qquad \mathbf x^TA\mathbf x=\sum_i\lambda_i y_i^2\;\text{ with }\;\mathbf y=Q^T\mathbf x$$

The core intuition here is that a symmetric matrix has perpendicular eigen-directions. In those directions the form is a plain sum of scaled squares.

*Example:* Find the maximum of $3x^2+4xy$ on $x^2+y^2=1$. The matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\2&0\end{pmatrix}$ with trace $3$ and determinant $-4$. The maximum is $4$.
$$\lambda^2-3\lambda-4=0\;\Rightarrow\;\lambda=4,\,-1$$

*Trap:* Taking the cross term $4xy$ itself as the off-diagonal entry. Each off-diagonal entry is half of the cross coefficient.

*Check:* The eigenvalues must add to the trace.

name: Nilpotent and Jordan structure
teach:
When a matrix has $N^k=0$ for some $k$, or a Jordan block structure or minimal polynomial is needed, find the smallest such $k$. The minimal polynomial is then $x^k$. A single Jordan block of size $s$ with eigenvalue $0$ has $N^{s-1}\neq0$ and $N^s=0$. The number of blocks is $\dim\ker N$, and the block sizes add up to $n$, so $\operatorname{rank}N=n-(\text{number of blocks})$.
$$N^k=0\;\Rightarrow\;\text{only eigenvalue }0,\qquad N^m\neq0\text{ for }m<k$$

The core intuition here is that a nilpotent matrix shifts vectors down a chain until they vanish. The chain length decides the smallest power that gives zero.

*Example:* A $4\times4$ Jordan block has ones on the superdiagonal. Its first, second and third powers are nonzero, so the minimal polynomial is $x^4$.
$$N^3\neq0,\qquad N^4=0,\qquad \dim\ker N=1$$

*Trap:* Concluding $N=0$ from $N^2=0$. A nonzero matrix can still square to zero.

*Check:* The index $k$ can never exceed the matrix size.

name: Divisibility and gcd
teach:
When two integers need a greatest common divisor or least common multiple, or you must test whether they share a factor, divide, keep the remainder, and repeat with the pair $(b,\text{remainder})$. Stop when the remainder is $0$. The last nonzero remainder is the gcd, and the lcm is $ab$ divided by the gcd. To count the integers up to $n$ coprime to $m$, count one block of $m$ consecutive integers, scale by the number of full blocks, and handle the leftover part.
$$\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(b,\;a\bmod b),\qquad \gcd(a,b)\cdot\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)=ab$$

The core intuition here is that a common divisor of $a$ and $b$ also divides the remainder of $a$ by $b$. So each division step keeps the gcd and shrinks the numbers.

*Example:* Find $\gcd(84,30)$ and the lcm. The steps below end with last nonzero remainder $6$, so the gcd is $6$ and the lcm is $\frac{84\cdot30}{6}=420$.
$$84=2\cdot30+24,\quad 30=1\cdot24+6,\quad 24=4\cdot6+0$$

*Trap:* Calling two numbers coprime because neither looks divisible by the other. Compare their prime factors.

*Check:* The gcd divides both numbers, and the lcm is a multiple of both.

name: Modular arithmetic
teach:
When a large sum, product or power must be reduced to a small remainder, or a congruence $ax\equiv b$ must be solved, reduce each factor first, then multiply and reduce again. To solve $ax\equiv b$, find an inverse of $a$ modulo $n$, which exists exactly when $\gcd(a,n)=1$, and multiply both sides by it. For a power, list powers of the base until one equals $1$, then reduce the exponent by that cycle length.
$$a\equiv b,\;c\equiv d\pmod n\;\Rightarrow\;a+c\equiv b+d,\quad ac\equiv bd$$

The core intuition here is that congruence modulo $n$ is compatible with addition and multiplication. You may reduce at every step without changing the final remainder.

*Example:* Solve $4x\equiv3\pmod{11}$. Since $4\cdot3=12\equiv1$, the inverse of $4$ is $3$.
$$x\equiv3\cdot3=9\pmod{11}$$

*Trap:* Dividing both sides by a number that shares a factor with $n$. Division is only valid by an invertible element.

*Check:* Substitute the answer back into the original congruence. Here $4\cdot9=36=33+3$.

name: Fermat, Euler, Wilson
teach:
When a power $a^k$ is taken modulo $n$ with $k$ large, or a factorial or totient appears, first check that the base is coprime to $n$. For a prime $p$ use $\varphi(p)=p-1$, and for $n=\prod p_i^{e_i}$ use $\varphi(n)=\prod p_i^{e_i-1}(p_i-1)$. Then divide the exponent by $\varphi(n)$, keep the remainder, and compute the base to that small exponent. Wilson's theorem works the same way, replacing a long factorial by $-1$ modulo a prime.
$$a^{\varphi(n)}\equiv1\pmod n\;\text{ if }\gcd(a,n)=1,\qquad (p-1)!\equiv-1\pmod p$$

The core intuition here is that powers of a unit modulo $n$ repeat with a cycle that divides $\varphi(n)$. So only the exponent modulo that cycle matters.

*Example:* Find $7^{50}\bmod 13$, where $\varphi(13)=12$ and $50=4\cdot12+2$.
$$7^{50}\equiv7^2=49\equiv10\pmod{13}$$

*Trap:* Using Fermat when the base is a multiple of $p$, or reducing the exponent by $p$ instead of $p-1$.

*Check:* Confirm the cycle directly. Since $7^2\equiv10$, $7^4\equiv100\equiv9$ and $7^6\equiv90\equiv-1$, we get $7^{12}\equiv1$ as promised.

name: Group definition and examples
teach:
When a set with a new operation is called a group, or an identity or inverse must be found, check closure, associativity, an identity $e$, and an inverse for every element. Solve $a*e=a$ for $e$, then solve $a*b=e$ for $b$. If a solution fails to exist for even one element, it is not a group. In $\mathbb Z_n$ under addition the inverse of $a$ is $n-a$. The units of $\mathbb Z_n$ under multiplication are the residues coprime to $n$, so there are $\varphi(n)$ of them.
$$a*e=e*a=a,\qquad a*a^{-1}=a^{-1}*a=e$$

The core intuition here is that the four axioms are exactly what is needed to solve equations like $a*x=b$. If one fails, some equation has no solution or too many.

*Example:* On $\mathbb Z$ define $a*b=a+b-3$. Closure and associativity hold, since both bracketings give $a+b+c-6$. The two equations below give the identity and the inverse, so $(\mathbb Z,*)$ is a group.
$$a+e-3=a\Rightarrow e=3,\qquad a+b-3=3\Rightarrow b=6-a$$

*Trap:* Assuming the old identity still works after the operation changes.

*Check:* Plug the identity back in on both sides.

name: Subgroups and cyclic groups
teach:
When a subset must be tested as a subgroup, or the order, generators or subgroups of a cyclic group are asked, use the subgroup test: it contains the identity, and $x,y\in H$ implies $xy^{-1}\in H$. In $\mathbb Z_n$, the generators are the $a$ with $\gcd(a,n)=1$. There is exactly one subgroup for each divisor of $n$, and $\varphi(d)$ elements of order $d$. In $\mathbb Z$, the subgroup $\langle n\rangle$ contains $a$ exactly when $n\mid a$.
$$\operatorname{ord}(a)=\frac{n}{\gcd(a,n)}\ \text{ in }\mathbb Z_n,\qquad \langle a\rangle=\{ka\}$$

The core intuition here is that a subgroup must stay closed under the operation and keep identities and inverses. A cyclic group is built by repeating one element.

*Example:* In $\mathbb Z_{18}$, find the order of $12$ and the number of generators.
$$\operatorname{ord}(12)=\frac{18}{\gcd(12,18)}=\frac{18}{6}=3,\qquad \varphi(18)=6$$

*Trap:* Forgetting inverses, so that $\{x\ge0\}$ passes closure but fails as a subgroup of $\mathbb Z$.

*Check:* The order of an element divides $n$.

name: Element order and Lagrange
teach:
When a question asks which orders are possible for a subgroup or an element, or uses $|G|$ divisibility, find the order of $g$ by listing powers until you return to the identity. Then test every divisor claim against $|G|$. Lagrange gives necessary conditions only. A cyclic group of order $n$ has $\varphi(d)$ elements of order $d$ for each divisor $d$ of $n$.
$$|H|\mid|G|,\qquad \operatorname{ord}(g)\mid|G|,\qquad \operatorname{ord}(g^k)=\frac{\operatorname{ord}(g)}{\gcd(k,\operatorname{ord}(g))}$$

The core intuition here is that cosets of a subgroup $H$ chop $G$ into equal-sized pieces of size $|H|$. So $|H|$ must divide $|G|$.

*Example:* In $\mathbb Z_{11}^\times$ of order $10$, find the order of $3$. The powers are $3,9,5,4,1$, so the order is $5$, which divides $10$.
$$3^5=243=22\cdot11+1\equiv1$$

*Trap:* Claiming a subgroup of every order dividing $|G|$. The group $A_4$ has order $12$ but no subgroup of order $6$.

*Check:* The order found divides $|G|$.

name: Permutation groups
teach:
When a permutation must be written in cycles, or its order, sign, or a count in $S_n$ or $A_n$ is needed, trace each point until it returns to find the cycles. Here $\ell$ is a cycle length. Even permutations have sign $+1$ and form $A_n$. The number of $k$-cycles in $S_n$ is $\frac{n!}{k\,(n-k)!}$, and every $3$-cycle is even.
$$\operatorname{ord}=\operatorname{lcm}(\text{cycle lengths}),\qquad \operatorname{sgn}=\prod(-1)^{\ell-1},\qquad |S_n|=n!,\ |A_n|=\tfrac{n!}{2}$$

The core intuition here is that disjoint cycles commute and act independently. So order and sign split cycle by cycle.

*Example:* Take $\sigma=(1\,2\,3)(4\,5)(6\,7\,8\,9)$ in $S_9$. So $\sigma$ is even and lies in $A_9$.
$$\operatorname{ord}\sigma=\operatorname{lcm}(3,2,4)=12,\qquad \operatorname{sgn}\sigma=(+1)(-1)(-1)=+1$$

*Trap:* Taking the lcm of the points moved instead of the cycle lengths.

*Check:* The cycle lengths of a permutation of $n$ points add to $n$, counting fixed points.

name: Dihedral and small groups
teach:
When symmetries of a regular polygon are asked about, or a small group must be identified, let $r$ be rotation by $\frac{2\pi}n$ and $s$ a reflection. The group $D_n$ has $n$ rotations and $n$ reflections, and each reflection has order $2$. Since $sr^k=r^{-k}s$, a product of two reflections is a rotation, and $r^k$ has order $\frac{n}{\gcd(n,k)}$. To name a small group, count elements of each order and test whether it is abelian. A group of order $4$ is $\mathbb Z_4$ or the Klein group $\mathbb Z_2^2$, which has three elements of order $2$. The group $D_4$ has order $8$ and five elements of order $2$.
$$D_n=\langle r,s\mid r^n=s^2=1,\;srs^{-1}=r^{-1}\rangle,\qquad |D_n|=2n$$

The core intuition here is that each symmetry is a rotation or a reflection. That fixes the whole structure with two generators.

*Example:* A group of order $6$ has an element of order $3$ and three elements of order $2$, and it is not abelian. The cyclic group $\mathbb Z_6$ has only one element of order $2$.
$$G\cong D_3\cong S_3$$

*Trap:* Calling $D_n$ abelian because the rotations commute, or confusing $D_4$ with $\mathbb Z_8$.

*Check:* The element orders must all divide $|G|$.

name: Cosets and normal subgroups
teach:
When a group must be split by a subgroup, cosets or index are counted, or normality is tested, list the left cosets $gH$, which partition $G$ into pieces of size $|H|$. To test normality, conjugate a generator of $N$ by each generator of $G$ and see if it stays in $N$. A subgroup of index $2$ is always normal.
$$[G:H]=\frac{|G|}{|H|},\qquad N\trianglelefteq G\iff gNg^{-1}=N\ \text{for all }g$$

The core intuition here is that normality is what makes coset multiplication well defined. Without it the quotient is not a group.

*Example:* Let $G=S_3$, generated by $(1\,2)$ and $(1\,2\,3)$, and $N=\{e,(1\,2\,3),(1\,3\,2)\}$, which is generated by $(1\,2\,3)$. Conjugating by $(1\,2\,3)$ changes nothing, and conjugating by $(1\,2)$ gives $(1\,3\,2)$. Both stay in $N$, so $N$ is normal.
$$(1\,2)(1\,2\,3)(1\,2)^{-1}=(1\,3\,2)\in N$$

*Trap:* Thinking normal means abelian. Normal subgroups exist in nonabelian groups.

*Check:* The index is $\frac{6}{3}=2$, and every subgroup of index $2$ is normal, which agrees.

name: Quotients and homomorphisms
teach:
When a map between groups is given, or a quotient group is named and its order or structure is wanted, check the operation rule first. Find the kernel as the preimage of the identity. The map is injective exactly when the kernel is trivial. Then read off the size of the image from the kernel, because the image has as many elements as the quotient $G/\ker\varphi$.
$$\varphi(xy)=\varphi(x)\varphi(y),\qquad G/\ker\varphi\cong\operatorname{im}\varphi,\qquad |G|=|\ker\varphi|\,|\operatorname{im}\varphi|$$

The core intuition here is that a homomorphism sends the structure of one group onto the other. The elements it kills form the kernel, and the quotient by the kernel is the image.

*Example:* Let $\varphi:\mathbb Z_{20}\to\mathbb Z_{20}$ be $x\mapsto5x$. The kernel is $\{0,4,8,12,16\}$ with $5$ elements. So $\mathbb Z_{20}/\ker\varphi\cong\mathbb Z_4$.
$$|\operatorname{im}\varphi|=\frac{20}{5}=4$$

*Trap:* Testing the map on one input only. The rule must hold for all pairs.

*Check:* Kernel size times image size must equal $|G|$.

name: Finite abelian groups
teach:
When all abelian groups of a given order must be listed or counted, or two abelian groups compared, factor the order. For each prime power $p^a$, list the partitions of $a$, and let $\pi(a)$ be how many there are. Each partition gives a product of cyclic $p$-groups. To compare groups, break every cyclic factor into prime-power parts. The order of $(a,b)$ is the lcm of the orders. In $\mathbb Z_n$ the equation $kx=0$ has $\gcd(k,n)$ solutions, so count elements of order dividing $k$ factor by factor.
$$|G|=\prod p_i^{a_i}\;\Rightarrow\;\#\text{types}=\prod_i \pi(a_i)$$

The core intuition here is that a finite abelian group splits into one piece for each prime. Within a prime, only the exponent pattern is free.

*Example:* Take order $72=2^3\cdot3^2$. The partitions of $3$ number $3$, and of $2$ number $2$.
$$3\cdot2=6\ \text{abelian groups, e.g. }\mathbb Z_8\times\mathbb Z_9,\ \mathbb Z_2^3\times\mathbb Z_3^2$$

*Trap:* Counting only cyclic groups, or assuming $\mathbb Z_a\times\mathbb Z_b$ is cyclic whenever the order is $ab$. It needs $\gcd(a,b)=1$.

*Check:* The factor orders multiply to $|G|$.

name: Group actions and Sylow
teach:
When a group of given order must have its Sylow subgroups counted, or an orbit or stabilizer size is needed, let $p^a$ be the largest power of $p$ dividing $|G|$ and let $n_p$ be the number of Sylow $p$-subgroups. List the divisors of the remaining part $\frac{|G|}{p^a}$ and keep those congruent to $1$ modulo $p$. A unique choice $n_p=1$ means the Sylow subgroup is normal. If several values survive, count elements of order $p$ to decide. For an action of $G$ on a set, the orbit of a point times its stabilizer gives $|G|$.
$$n_p\equiv1\pmod p,\qquad n_p\mid\frac{|G|}{p^a},\qquad |G|=|\mathrm{orbit}|\cdot|\mathrm{stab}|$$

The core intuition here is that counting arguments restrict how many subgroups of a prime power order can fit. Often only one number survives, which forces normality.

*Example:* Take order $20=4\cdot5$. For $p=5$, $n_5$ divides $4$ and is $1$ modulo $5$. So the Sylow $5$-subgroup is normal.
$$n_5\in\{1,2,4\},\ n_5\equiv1\pmod5\;\Rightarrow\;n_5=1$$

*Trap:* Assuming Sylow gives a unique subgroup for every prime. Uniqueness needs the count to be $1$.

*Check:* The count $n_p$ divides $|G|$.

name: Rings and ideals
teach:
When a subset of a ring may be an ideal, or units, zero divisors or the ring type are asked, check that $0\in I$, closure under subtraction, and absorption by every $r\in R$. In $\mathbb Z_n$, the units are the residues coprime to $n$. A nonzero $a$ with $ab=0$ for some nonzero $b$ is a zero divisor, and in $\mathbb Z_n$ every nonzero nonunit is one. The ideal $\langle a\rangle$ of $\mathbb Z_n$ has $\frac{n}{\gcd(a,n)}$ elements.
$$I\ \text{ideal}:\quad a,b\in I\Rightarrow a-b\in I,\qquad r\in R,\ a\in I\Rightarrow ra\in I$$

The core intuition here is that an ideal absorbs multiplication, so quotients by it stay rings. Units and zero divisors show whether you can cancel.

*Example:* In $\mathbb Z_{14}$, find the units and test $7$. So $7$ is a zero divisor, and $\mathbb Z_{14}$ is not a domain.
$$\text{units}=\{1,3,5,9,11,13\},\qquad 7\cdot2=14\equiv0$$

*Trap:* Checking closure under addition only and skipping absorption.

*Check:* The count of units equals $\varphi(n)$.

name: Domains, PIDs, UFDs
teach:
When a ring must be placed in the chain below, or a factorization is counted, remember that a domain has no zero divisors and that in a UFD every nonzero nonunit factors uniquely into irreducibles. The inclusions do not reverse. In $\mathbb Z[i]$ the norm $N(a+bi)=a^2+b^2$ is multiplicative, and a unit has norm $1$. To count the positive divisors of an integer, add one to each exponent in its prime factorization and multiply, where $d(n)$ is the number of divisors.
$$\text{field}\subset\text{ED}\subset\text{PID}\subset\text{UFD}\subset\text{domain},\qquad d(p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_k^{a_k})=\prod(a_i+1)$$

The core intuition here is that each class adds one property needed for unique factoring. Knowing the chain tells you which statements follow.

*Example:* Count the positive divisors of $450=2\cdot3^2\cdot5^2$.
$$d(450)=(1+1)(2+1)(2+1)=18$$

*Trap:* Believing a UFD is always a PID. The ring $\mathbb Z[x]$ is a UFD, but the ideal $(2,x)$ is not principal.

*Check:* Divisors pair up as $d$ and $\frac nd$, so the count is even unless $n$ is a square.

name: Irreducible polynomials
teach:
When a polynomial must be factored or declared irreducible over a field such as $\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb Z_p$, test for roots. Over $\mathbb Z_p$, test every residue $0,\dots,p-1$. Over $\mathbb Q$, test only the rational roots $\frac{r}{s}$ with $r$ dividing the constant term and $s$ the leading coefficient. For degree $4$ and up, no root is not enough, so factor with differences of squares and known patterns first.
$$f(a)=0\iff (x-a)\mid f(x),\qquad \deg f\in\{2,3\}\text{ irreducible}\iff\text{no root}$$

The core intuition here is that a linear factor is the same thing as a root. For degree $2$ or $3$, no linear factor means no factor at all.

*Example:* Is $x^2+2$ irreducible over $\mathbb Z_5$? No root exists, so the quadratic is irreducible.
$$f(0)=2,\ f(1)=3,\ f(2)=1,\ f(3)=1,\ f(4)=3$$

*Trap:* Skipping some residues, or declaring a quartic irreducible because it has no root.

*Check:* The degree must be $2$ or $3$ for the root test to decide.

name: Field extensions
teach:
When the degree of an extension is asked, or a quotient $F[x]/(f)$ must be recognised, write a polynomial with root $\alpha$ and prove it irreducible over $F$, where $m_\alpha$ is the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$. Then its degree is the answer. By Eisenstein, if a prime $p$ divides every non-leading coefficient and $p^2$ does not divide the constant term, $f$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$. For a tower, find each step and multiply. If $[F(\alpha):F]$ and $[F(\beta):F]$ are coprime, then $[F(\alpha,\beta):F]$ is their product.
$$[F(\alpha):F]=\deg m_\alpha,\qquad [K:F]=[K:E]\,[E:F]$$

The core intuition here is that adjoining a root of an irreducible polynomial of degree $d$ adds exactly $d$ independent directions. Degrees multiply through towers.

*Example:* Find $[\mathbb Q(\sqrt[4]{2}):\mathbb Q]$. The polynomial $x^4-2$ has root $\sqrt[4]{2}$ and is irreducible by Eisenstein at $2$.
$$[\mathbb Q(\sqrt[4]{2}):\mathbb Q]=4$$

*Trap:* Using the degree of a polynomial without checking that it is irreducible.

*Check:* The total degree is divisible by each step degree.

name: Real numbers and sup/inf
teach:
When a set of reals is bounded and you need its least upper bound or greatest lower bound, or you must say whether a maximum exists, first guess the largest value the set approaches. Then test the approximation clause below, which says that nothing smaller is an upper bound. The supremum belongs to the set only if some member reaches it. For a sequence, compare terms to see whether a largest one is reached, as in a finite set. The infimum works the same way from below.
$$s=\sup S\iff s\text{ is an upper bound and }\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists x\in S:\ x>s-\varepsilon$$

The core intuition here is that the reals have no gaps. Every nonempty set that is bounded above has a least upper bound, which the rationals fail to give.

*Example:* Find $\sup\{\frac{2n}{n+1}: n\ge1\}$. The terms are $1,\frac43,\frac32,\dots$ and they climb toward $2$.
$$\frac{2n}{n+1}=2-\frac{2}{n+1}<2,\qquad \sup=2,\ \text{not attained}$$

*Trap:* Treating the supremum as a maximum. A set can have a supremum and no largest member.

*Check:* The supremum is at least every element, and nothing smaller is an upper bound.

name: Sequence convergence proofs
teach:
When a limit $a_n\to L$ must be found, or proved from the definition, find it by dividing top and bottom by the highest power of $n$. For a difference of roots, multiply by the conjugate, and for a bounded numerator over $n$, squeeze. To prove it, fix $\varepsilon$ and solve $|a_n-L|<\varepsilon$ for $n$. Set $N$ to be any integer past that threshold.
$$a_n\to L\iff\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists N:\ n\ge N\Rightarrow|a_n-L|<\varepsilon$$

The core intuition here is that convergence says the terms get and stay within any chosen distance of $L$. The proof picks the distance first and then finds how far out to go.

*Example:* Prove $\frac{n}{n+4}\to1$. The gap is small once $n$ is large, so take $N$ larger than $\frac4\varepsilon$.
$$\left|\frac{n}{n+4}-1\right|=\frac{4}{n+4}<\varepsilon\iff n>\frac4\varepsilon-4$$

*Trap:* Choosing $N$ before $\varepsilon$, or treating $\varepsilon$ as one specific number.

*Check:* The $N$ you found must grow as $\varepsilon$ shrinks.

name: Cauchy sequences and Bolzano-Weierstrass
teach:
When a sequence must be shown to converge without naming its limit, or a bounded sequence needs a convergent piece, remember that in $\mathbb R$ Cauchy means convergent. Bolzano-Weierstrass says a bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence. To list the subsequential limits, split the index by parity or by residue class and find the limit of each piece. The limsup is the largest subsequential limit and the liminf is the smallest.
$$(a_n)\text{ Cauchy}\iff\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists N:\ m,n\ge N\Rightarrow|a_m-a_n|<\varepsilon$$

The core intuition here is that in the reals, terms that crowd together must settle on a point, because there is no gap to fall into.

*Example:* Find the subsequential limits of $a_n=\cos\left(\frac{2n\pi}{3}\right)$, whose values cycle through $-\frac12,-\frac12,1$. The sequence is bounded but does not converge.
$$\text{limits}=\{-\tfrac12,\,1\},\qquad \limsup a_n=1,\ \liminf a_n=-\tfrac12$$

*Trap:* Claiming a bounded sequence converges when only a subsequence does.

*Check:* Each subsequential limit must lie between the infimum and supremum of the terms.

name: Continuity (epsilon-delta)
teach:
When continuity at a point must be proved, or a $\delta$ must be found for a given $\varepsilon$, factor $|f(x)-f(c)|$ as $|x-c|$ times something. Bound the other factor by assuming $|x-c|<1$. Then pick $\delta$ as the smaller of $1$ and $\varepsilon$ divided by that bound. For a reciprocal such as $\frac1x$, the cap must also keep $x$ away from $0$.
$$\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0:\ |x-c|<\delta\Rightarrow|f(x)-f(c)|<\varepsilon$$

The core intuition here is that continuity says a small enough input change forces a small output change. The proof turns the output gap into a bound on the input gap.

*Example:* Show $f(x)=x^2$ is continuous at $c=3$. If $|x-3|<1$, then $|x+3|<7$. So take $\delta=\min\left(1,\tfrac\varepsilon7\right)$.
$$|x^2-9|=|x-3||x+3|<7|x-3|<\varepsilon\ \text{ when }\ |x-3|<\tfrac\varepsilon7$$

*Trap:* Leaving out the cap at $1$, so the extra factor is not controlled.

*Check:* The $\delta$ shrinks as $\varepsilon$ shrinks and never depends on $x$.

name: Uniform continuity
teach:
When a question asks whether one $\delta$ works for all points of a set, not just near one point, bound the derivative on the set. If it is bounded, $f$ is Lipschitz and uniformly continuous. A continuous function on a closed bounded interval is always uniformly continuous. If the derivative is unbounded, look for two sequences that approach each other while the outputs stay apart.
$$|f'|\le L\Rightarrow|f(x)-f(y)|\le L|x-y|\Rightarrow\delta=\frac\varepsilon L$$

The core intuition here is that a function that gets steeper without bound needs a smaller $\delta$ further out. A bounded slope prevents that.

*Example:* Test $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ on $[1,\infty)$, whose derivative is $\frac1{2\sqrt x}\le\frac12$. So $f$ is uniformly continuous there.
$$\delta=2\varepsilon\ \text{ works for every point}$$

*Trap:* Calling $x^2$ uniformly continuous on $\mathbb R$ because it is continuous.

*Check:* Use the definition directly. For $x,y\ge1$, $|\sqrt x-\sqrt y|=\frac{|x-y|}{\sqrt x+\sqrt y}\le\frac{|x-y|}{2}$, which matches $L=\frac12$.

name: Consequences of continuity
teach:
When a continuous function needs a root, a maximum or minimum, or a count of solutions, evaluate $f$ at the endpoints and look for a sign change. For uniqueness, show $f$ is strictly monotone. The extreme value theorem needs a closed bounded interval and continuity. To find the extremes, compare $f$ at the endpoints and at the critical points inside.
$$f\in C[a,b],\ f(a)f(b)<0\Rightarrow\exists c\in(a,b):\ f(c)=0$$

The core intuition here is that a continuous graph has no jumps. It must pass through every value between two outputs, and on a closed bounded interval it reaches its top and bottom.

*Example:* Show $x^3+2x-5=0$ has exactly one real root, with $f(x)=x^3+2x-5$. A sign change gives a root, and strict increase gives only one.
$$f(1)=-2<0,\quad f(2)=7>0,\quad f'(x)=3x^2+2>0$$

*Trap:* Using the extreme value theorem on an open interval, where the maximum may not be attained.

*Check:* Narrow the interval. Here $f(1.3)\approx-0.2$ and $f(1.4)\approx0.54$, so the root is near $1.3$, inside $(1,2)$.

name: Differentiation theory
teach:
When you need a point where the derivative equals a given slope, or must judge a statement about zeros of $f'$, first check that $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. Then compute the average slope, set $f'(x)$ equal to it, and solve. Rolle's theorem is the case $f(a)=f(b)$, where the slope is $0$.
$$f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\ \text{ for some }c\in(a,b)$$

The core intuition here is that if a function leaves and returns to the same height, somewhere its slope must be zero. The mean value theorem tilts that picture.

*Example:* Find $c$ for $f(x)=x^3$ on $[0,2]$, where the average slope is $\frac{8-0}{2}=4$. Only the positive root lies in $(0,2)$.
$$3c^2=4\Rightarrow c=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\approx1.15$$

*Trap:* Thinking $f'(c)=0$ forces an extremum. The function $x^3$ at $0$ has zero slope and no extremum.

*Check:* The point $c$ must lie strictly inside the interval.

name: Riemann integrability
teach:
When a function's integrability is in question, or an upper, lower or Riemann sum is computed, split the interval by a partition $P$ and let $M_i$ and $m_i$ be the supremum and infimum of $f$ on piece $i$, which has width $\Delta x_i$. For an increasing $f$, $M_i$ is at the right end and $m_i$ at the left. A bounded function whose discontinuities form a countable set is integrable.
$$U(f,P)=\sum M_i\,\Delta x_i,\qquad L(f,P)=\sum m_i\,\Delta x_i$$

The core intuition here is that a function is integrable when upper and lower sums squeeze together. Wild jumping everywhere prevents that squeeze.

*Example:* Take $f(x)=2x$ on $[0,1]$ with the partition $\{0,\frac12,1\}$. The true integral is $1$, between the two sums.
$$U=\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(2)=\tfrac32,\qquad L=\tfrac12(0)+\tfrac12(1)=\tfrac12$$

*Trap:* Using the right endpoint for the infimum of an increasing function.

*Check:* The lower sum never exceeds the upper sum.

name: Series convergence theory
teach:
When a series must be shown to converge or diverge, or summed in closed form, check the terms first. If they do not tend to $0$, the series diverges. Then match a known type. Split fractions to telescope, or compare with a geometric or $p$-series. A geometric tail is $\sum_{n>N}r^n=\frac{r^{N+1}}{1-r}$.
$$\sum_{n\ge0}ar^n=\frac{a}{1-r}\ (|r|<1),\qquad \sum a_n\text{ converges}\Rightarrow a_n\to0$$

The core intuition here is that a sum converges only if its partial sums settle. Terms that do not shrink to zero rule that out, and comparing with a known series settles the rest.

*Example:* Sum $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{1}{n(n+2)}$ by writing each term as a difference.
$$\frac{1}{n(n+2)}=\frac12\left(\frac1n-\frac1{n+2}\right),\qquad S=\frac12\left(1+\frac12\right)=\frac34$$

*Trap:* Concluding convergence from $a_n\to0$. The harmonic series has terms tending to $0$ and diverges.

*Check:* A positive series must have a positive sum, bigger than its first term.

name: Uniform convergence
teach:
When a sequence or series of functions converges and you must decide if the convergence is uniform or if continuity survives, find the pointwise limit $f$. Then compute the supremum of the gap, using calculus if needed. If it tends to $0$, convergence is uniform. For series, use the M-test with bounds $M_n$ that do not depend on $x$ and have $\sum M_n<\infty$.
$$f_n\to f\ \text{uniformly}\iff\sup_{x\in A}|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$$

The core intuition here is that pointwise convergence lets the slow region move around. Uniform convergence forces the worst gap over the whole set to shrink.

*Example:* Let $f_n(x)=xe^{-nx}$ on $[0,\infty)$, with pointwise limit $0$. Also $f_n'=e^{-nx}(1-nx)=0$ at $x=\frac1n$, so the convergence is uniform.
$$\sup_{x\ge0}f_n(x)=f_n\!\left(\tfrac1n\right)=\frac{1}{en}\to0$$

*Trap:* Checking the pointwise limit only.

*Check:* For $n=1$ the maximum of $xe^{-x}$ is $\frac1e\approx0.37$, which matches $\frac{1}{en}$.

name: Metric spaces and open/closed sets
teach:
When a subset of a metric space is called open, closed, or has its interior, closure or boundary asked, test the ball at each point, especially at endpoints. The closure adds limit points and the interior removes boundary points. The boundary is closure minus interior. A closed ball is all $y$ with $d(x,y)\le r$, so its shape follows the metric. The diameter is the supremum of $d(x,y)$ over pairs. In $\mathbb R$, removing $k$ points leaves $k+1$ pieces.
$$U\text{ open}\iff\forall x\in U\ \exists r>0:\ B(x,r)\subset U,\qquad F\text{ closed}\iff F^c\text{ open}$$

The core intuition here is that open means every point has breathing room and closed means no limit points escape. Complements swap the two.

*Example:* In $\mathbb R$, let $S=[0,1)\cup\{3\}$. So $S$ is neither open nor closed.
$$\operatorname{int}S=(0,1),\quad \bar S=[0,1]\cup\{3\},\quad \partial S=\{0,1,3\}$$

*Trap:* Thinking a set is either open or closed. A half-open interval is neither.

*Check:* The set is not open because no ball about $0$ stays inside $S$, and not closed because the limit point $1$ is missing.

name: Compactness and connectedness
teach:
When a claim involves compactness or connectedness, or asks which sets have these properties, test closedness and boundedness separately. In $\mathbb R$, connected sets are exactly intervals. For components, remove the excluded points from an interval and count the pieces. A decreasing chain of nonempty compact sets has a nonempty intersection.
$$K\subset\mathbb R\text{ compact}\iff K\text{ closed and bounded},\qquad f\text{ continuous}\Rightarrow f(K)\text{ compact}$$

The core intuition here is that compact sets have no escape routes, so continuous functions on them behave well. Connected sets have no gaps, so they cannot be split.

*Example:* Is $\left[0,1\right)\cup\{2\}$ compact or connected?
$$\text{not closed }(1\text{ is a limit point not in the set})\ \Rightarrow\ \text{not compact},\qquad \text{two pieces}\Rightarrow\text{not connected}$$

*Trap:* Calling $(0,1]$ compact because it is bounded, or $\mathbb R$ compact because it is closed.

*Check:* A compact subset of $\mathbb R$ has a maximum and a minimum.

name: General topology
teach:
When a family of sets is claimed to be a topology, or a property is claimed to hold in every topological space, check $\emptyset$ and $X$ first. On a finite set, check unions of all pairs, then intersections of all pairs. One failure ends the test. To count topologies, list the families that contain $\emptyset$ and $X$ and test each. Discrete means every subset is open, giving $2^{|X|}$ open sets, and indiscrete means only $\emptyset$ and $X$ are open.
$$\emptyset,X\in\tau,\qquad \bigcup_{i}U_i\in\tau,\qquad U\cap V\in\tau$$

The core intuition here is that a topology only needs a few rules. Those rules allow strange spaces where metric intuition fails.

*Example:* Is $\tau=\{\emptyset,\{1,2\},\{3\},X\}$ a topology on $X=\{1,2,3,4\}$? It is not, because the union below is missing.
$$\{1,2\}\cup\{3\}=\{1,2,3\}\notin\tau$$

*Trap:* Assuming points are closed in every topology. That holds for metric spaces, not for all topologies.

*Check:* A topology on a $4$-point set has at most $2^4=16$ open sets, and this family has only $4$, so size alone cannot settle it.

name: Countability
teach:
When a set must be classified as finite, countably infinite or uncountable, or subsets are counted, try to build an explicit list. Functions from $A$ to $B$ number $|B|^{|A|}$, and injective ones number $\frac{|B|!}{(|B|-|A|)!}$. Countable unions and finite products of countable sets are countable. To show a set is uncountable, run Cantor's diagonal argument, where any list misses a number that differs from the $n$th entry in its $n$th digit.
$$|\mathcal P(S)|=2^{|S|},\qquad \mathbb N,\ \mathbb Z,\ \mathbb Q\ \text{countable},\qquad \mathbb R\ \text{uncountable}$$

The core intuition here is that countable means the elements can be listed in a sequence. Many familiar infinite sets can be, and a few cannot.

*Example:* Is the set of all finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ countable? There are countably many of each size, so it is countable.
$$\bigcup_{k\ge0}\{\text{subsets of size }k\}\ \text{is a countable union of countable sets}$$

*Trap:* Assuming every infinite set is uncountable.

*Check:* An infinite subset of a countable set is still countable.

name: Standard counterexamples
teach:
When a claim says a property passes through a limit, a sum, or an integral, match the claim to a standard example. A pointwise limit of continuous functions may be discontinuous. A uniform limit of differentiable functions need not be differentiable, and its derivative need not converge.
$$x^n\to\begin{cases}0&x<1\\1&x=1\end{cases}\ \text{on }[0,1],\qquad \frac{\sin nx}{n}\to0\ \text{but}\ \cos nx\not\to0$$

The core intuition here is that many natural swaps of limits fail. A small stock of examples tells you which swaps are unsafe.

*Example:* Can a uniform limit of differentiable functions fail to be differentiable? Take $f_n(x)=\sqrt{x^2+1/n^2}$. Each $f_n$ is smooth, and the gap to $|x|$ is largest at $x=0$. So $f_n\to|x|$ uniformly, but $|x|$ has a corner at $0$.
$$\sup_x\left|\sqrt{x^2+\tfrac1{n^2}}-|x|\right|=\frac1n\to0$$

*Trap:* Reading a pointwise limit as a uniform one.

*Check:* The claimed property must fail in a named, checkable example.

name: Counting principles
teach:
When a problem asks how many arrangements, selections or outcomes there are, first fix whether order matters and whether repeats are allowed. Ordered picks of $k$ from $n$ use the first formula, unordered picks use the second, and independent stages multiply. To seat people with two side by side, glue them into one block, count the block arrangements, then multiply by the orders inside the block. To give $k$ identical items to $n$ people, any amount each, the count is $\binom{k+n-1}{n-1}$. When a condition such as "at least one" is awkward, count the complement and subtract it from the total.
$$P(n,k)=\frac{n!}{(n-k)!},\qquad \binom nk=\frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}$$

The core intuition here is that counting problems come down to two choices: whether order matters and whether repeats are allowed. Once those are fixed, a standard formula applies.

*Example:* Choose a team of $2$ from $6$ men and $4$ women with at least one woman.
$$\binom{10}{2}-\binom62=45-15=30$$

*Trap:* Dividing by $k!$ when the roles are distinct, or counting the same group once for each order.

*Check:* The answer cannot exceed the total number of unrestricted choices.

name: Inclusion-exclusion and pigeonhole
teach:
When a count joins overlapping sets with "or", add the sizes of the single sets, subtract the sizes of the pairwise overlaps, then add back the triple overlap. Divisible by two numbers means divisible by their lcm. When a problem asks what is guaranteed, use the pigeonhole principle. If $N$ objects go into $m$ boxes, some box holds at least $\lceil N/m\rceil$ of them, and to force $k$ objects into one box you need $m(k-1)+1$ objects.
$$|A\cup B\cup C|=\sum|A|-\sum|A\cap B|+|A\cap B\cap C|$$

The core intuition here is that adding set sizes counts the overlaps twice, so they must be subtracted. For guarantees, if every box held few objects, the total would be too small.

*Example:* How many integers from $1$ to $30$ are divisible by $2$, $3$ or $5$? The other $8$ are coprime to $30$.
$$(15+10+6)-(5+3+2)+1=22$$

*Trap:* Stopping after the pairs and forgetting to add the triple back.

*Check:* The union is at least as large as the biggest single set and at most the total. Here $15\le22\le30$.

name: Recurrences
teach:
When a sequence is defined from earlier terms and you want a closed form or a far term, first decide the type. For a small index, just compute the terms one by one. For $a_n=ca_{n-1}$ the answer is $a_0c^n$. For a two-step linear recurrence, replace $a_n$ by $r^n$ and divide out the common power to get a quadratic. Solve it for $r_1$ and $r_2$ and write the general form with unknowns $A$ and $B$. Plug in the first two terms to get two equations, and solve them. To count strings, split by the last symbol to get the recurrence.
$$a_n=c_1a_{n-1}+c_2a_{n-2}\ \Rightarrow\ r^2=c_1r+c_2,\qquad a_n=Ar_1^n+Br_2^n$$

The core intuition here is that a power $r^n$ solves a linear recurrence when $r$ satisfies the matching polynomial. Combining such powers fits any starting values.

*Example:* Solve $a_n=a_{n-1}+6a_{n-2}$ with $a_0=1$ and $a_1=2$. Then $r^2=r+6$ gives $r=3,-2$.
$$A+B=1,\ 3A-2B=2\ \Rightarrow\ a_n=\frac{4\cdot3^n+(-2)^n}{5}$$

*Trap:* An off-by-one slip in the index of the starting values.

*Check:* Compute $a_2$ both ways. The recurrence gives $8$, and the formula must agree.

name: Graph theory basics
teach:
When a problem gives vertices, edges and degrees, or names a complete, bipartite or tree graph, add the degrees and halve to count edges. The sum must be even, so the number of odd-degree vertices is even. A tree on $v$ vertices has $v-1$ edges.
$$\sum_v\deg v=2|E|,\qquad |E(K_n)|=\binom n2,\qquad |E(K_{m,n})|=mn$$

The core intuition here is that each edge touches exactly two vertices. That one fact links the degrees to the edge count.

*Example:* A simple graph on $5$ vertices has degrees $4,3,3,2,2$. The degrees add to an even number, so the list is possible, and halving gives the edge count. A list such as $3,3,3,2,2$ sums to $13$, which is odd, so it is impossible.
$$4+3+3+2+2=14\ \Rightarrow\ |E|=7$$

*Trap:* Using $n(n-1)$ edges for $K_n$, which counts each edge twice.

*Check:* No degree exceeds the number of other vertices.

name: Euler, Hamilton, coloring, planarity
teach:
When a question asks about Euler circuits, Hamilton cycles, colorings or planarity, use the local test for each. An Euler circuit uses every edge once, and a Hamilton cycle uses every vertex once. The planar formulas apply to connected simple planar graphs with $v\ge3$ vertices, $e$ edges and $f$ faces. The chromatic number is the fewest colors with adjacent vertices different. Bipartite graphs need $2$ colors, and an odd cycle needs $3$.
$$\text{Euler circuit}\iff\text{connected, all degrees even}$$
$$v-e+f=2,\qquad e\le3v-6$$

The core intuition here is that each property has a local test. Euler circuits need an even number of edges at every vertex, and planar graphs cannot have too many edges.

*Example:* Test $K_7$, where every degree is $6$.
$$\text{Euler: yes},\qquad e=21>3\cdot7-6=15\Rightarrow\text{not planar},\qquad \chi=7$$

*Trap:* Mixing up the Euler circuit, which covers edges, with the Hamilton cycle, which covers vertices.

*Check:* A planar graph can never contain $K_5$.

name: Algorithms and complexity
teach:
When a question asks for the running time of a loop or a divide-and-conquer routine, or for a search or shortest-path method, write the recurrence, or sum the loop counts. In the recurrence below, $a$ subproblems of size $\frac nb$ are solved and $f(n)$ is the extra work. Expand a few levels, count the work per level, and multiply by the number of levels. Dijkstra needs nonnegative edge weights, and a spanning tree on $v$ vertices has $v-1$ edges.
$$T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n),\qquad \text{binary search: }\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\text{ comparisons}$$

The core intuition here is that running time is the number of basic steps. Halving the input each step reaches size $1$ after about $\log_2n$ steps.

*Example:* Solve $T(n)=3T(n/3)+n$ with $T(1)=0$ for $n=9$. Each of the $2$ levels does $n=9$ work.
$$T(3)=3,\ T(9)=3\cdot3+9=18=9\log_39$$

*Trap:* Treating $\log n$ as a cost per element, or running Dijkstra on negative weights.

*Check:* Predict one more step. The formula $n\log_3n$ gives $27\cdot3=81$ at $n=27$, and the recurrence gives $T(27)=3\cdot18+27=81$.

name: Probability basics
teach:
When a problem gives equally likely outcomes, or builds events with "and", "or" and "given", count favorable outcomes over total outcomes. Independence means $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. For "at least one", try $1-P(\text{none})$. Draws without replacement use $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B\mid A)$.
$$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B),\qquad P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$$

The core intuition here is that probability is a share of a total. Overlaps must not be counted twice, and conditioning shrinks the total to the given event.

*Example:* Roll two fair dice and find the probability of at least one six.
$$1-\left(\frac56\right)^2=1-\frac{25}{36}=\frac{11}{36}$$

*Trap:* Multiplying the probabilities of events that are not independent, or adding events that overlap.

*Check:* Count directly. Of the $36$ outcomes, $6+6-1=11$ contain a six.

name: Random variables
teach:
When a random numeric quantity has a known distribution and its mean or spread is asked, compute $E[X]$ and $E[X^2]$ in two separate sums, where $x$ runs over the values and $P(x)$ is the probability of each. Then subtract the square of the first from the second to get the variance. Expectation is linear, so $E[aX+b]=aE[X]+b$, and shifting $X$ by a constant leaves the spread unchanged. For $X$ uniform on $\{1,\dots,n\}$, $\operatorname{Var}X=\frac{n^2-1}{12}$.
$$E[X]=\sum xP(x),\qquad \operatorname{Var}X=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}X$$

The core intuition here is that the mean is a weighted average of the values. Variance measures the average squared distance from that mean.

*Example:* Let $X$ take the values $1,2,4$ with probabilities $0.5,0.3,0.2$.
$$E[X]=0.5+0.6+0.8=1.9,\quad E[X^2]=0.5+1.2+3.2=4.9,\quad \operatorname{Var}X=4.9-3.61=1.29$$

*Trap:* Writing $(E[X])^2$ for $E[X^2]$, or adding $b$ to the variance when shifting by $b$.

*Check:* Use the definition. $0.5(0.81)+0.3(0.01)+0.2(4.41)=0.405+0.003+0.882=1.29$.

name: Common distributions
teach:
When a problem names a standard model such as binomial, geometric, uniform or Poisson, identify the model, read off its parameters, then substitute. For the binomial, $n$ is the number of independent trials and $p$ the chance of success on each. The geometric counts trials up to and including the first success, and its mean is $\frac1p$. The uniform on $[a,b]$ has mean $\frac{a+b}2$, and an interval's probability is proportional to its length. The Poisson with mean $\lambda$ has variance $\lambda$, so $E[X^2]=\lambda+\lambda^2$.
$$X\sim B(n,p):\ P(k)=\binom nkp^k(1-p)^{n-k},\ E=np,\ \operatorname{Var}=np(1-p)$$
$$X\sim\text{Poisson}(\lambda):\ P(k)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}$$

The core intuition here is that each model packages a typical situation. Matching the situation lets you use its known formulas instead of summing from scratch.

*Example:* Let $X\sim B(5,\frac13)$ and find $P(X=2)$.
$$\binom52\left(\frac13\right)^2\left(\frac23\right)^3=10\cdot\frac19\cdot\frac8{27}=\frac{80}{243}$$

*Trap:* Using the number of failures when the geometric mean $\frac1p$ counts trials.

*Check:* Binomial probabilities over $k=0,\dots,n$ must sum to $1$.

name: Statistics essentials
teach:
When a question asks for a mean, median, sample spread, or a fitted line, let $\bar x$ and $\bar y$ be the means, $S_{xy}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)$, and $S_{xx}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2$. The fitted line is $y=a+bx$, and it always passes through the point of means. The median is the middle value, or the average of the middle two.
$$s^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2,\qquad b=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}},\qquad a=\bar y-b\bar x$$

The core intuition here is that a sample mean sits closer to the data than the true mean does, and dividing by $n-1$ corrects for that. The fitted line balances the data around its means.

*Example:* Fit a line to $(1,1),(2,3),(3,4)$, whose means are $\bar x=2$ and $\bar y=\frac83$.
$$S_{xy}=\tfrac53+0+\tfrac43=3,\quad S_{xx}=2,\quad b=\tfrac32,\quad a=\tfrac83-3=-\tfrac13$$

*Trap:* Dividing by $n$ when sample variance is asked.

*Check:* The line must pass through the point of means. At $x=2$ it gives $-\frac13+3=\frac83$.

name: Complex arithmetic and polar form
teach:
When a problem uses numbers $a+bi$, their size or conjugates, or asks for a power or quotient, multiply out and use $i^2=-1$. Here $\bar w$ is the conjugate, found by flipping the sign of the imaginary part, and $r$ and $\theta$ are the modulus and angle. To divide, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator, so the denominator becomes real. For powers, switch to polar form, where $z^n=r^ne^{in\theta}$.
$$|a+bi|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2},\qquad \frac{z}{w}=\frac{z\bar w}{|w|^2},\qquad z=re^{i\theta}$$

The core intuition here is that complex numbers are points in a plane. Rectangular form adds easily, and polar form multiplies easily.

*Example:* Compute $\frac{7+i}{1-2i}$.
$$\frac{(7+i)(1+2i)}{5}=\frac{7+15i-2}{5}=1+3i$$

*Trap:* Using $\sqrt a+\sqrt b$ for the modulus, or losing the sign from $i^2=-1$.

*Check:* Multiply the answer by the denominator and recover the numerator.

name: Analytic functions
teach:
When a function $f=u+iv$ is given and you must test whether it is analytic or find a missing part, compute the four partial derivatives, where $x$ and $y$ are the real and imaginary parts of $z$. Both equations below must hold, and then $f'=u_x+iv_x$. To find $v$ from $u$, integrate $v_y=u_x$ in $y$ and fix the leftover function of $x$ using the second equation.
$$u_x=v_y,\qquad u_y=-v_x$$

The core intuition here is that complex differentiability needs the same limit from every direction. That forces two linked equations between $u$ and $v$.

*Example:* Given $u=2xy+y$, find $v$. The two equations give $v=y^2-x^2-x$, and then $f=-i(z^2+z)$.
$$v_y=u_x=2y\Rightarrow v=y^2+h(x),\qquad -v_x=u_y=2x+1\Rightarrow h(x)=-x^2-x$$

*Trap:* Checking one equation only, or assuming any formula in $x$ and $y$ is analytic.

*Check:* The part you found must satisfy the second equation too.

name: Contour integrals and residues
teach:
When a closed-curve integral of a function with isolated poles is asked, list the poles by solving for the zeros of the denominator. Keep those inside the curve $C$, traversed counterclockwise, and sum their residues. If none are inside, the integral is $0$. For a simple pole, the residue is $\lim_{z\to z_0}(z-z_0)f(z)$. For $f=\frac gh$ with $h(z_0)=0$, $h'(z_0)\neq0$ and $g(z_0)\neq0$, it equals $\frac{g(z_0)}{h'(z_0)}$.
$$\oint_Cf\,dz=2\pi i\sum\operatorname{Res}_{\text{inside}},\qquad \operatorname{Res}_{z_0}\frac gh=\frac{g(z_0)}{h'(z_0)}$$

The core intuition here is that only the poles trapped inside the curve contribute. Each pole adds its residue, scaled by $2\pi i$.

*Example:* Take $C:\ |z-2i|=1$ and $f=\frac1{z^2+4}$, where only $z=2i$ is inside.
$$\operatorname{Res}_{2i}=\frac1{2z}\Big|_{2i}=\frac1{4i},\qquad \oint_Cf\,dz=2\pi i\cdot\frac1{4i}=\frac\pi2$$

*Trap:* Counting a pole outside the curve, dropping the factor $2\pi i$, or running the curve clockwise, which flips the sign.

*Check:* The limit formula must agree. $\frac{z-2i}{(z-2i)(z+2i)}\to\frac{1}{4i}$ as $z\to2i$.

name: Mobius maps and zeros
teach:
When a fractional linear map is given, first check that $ad-bc\neq0$, since otherwise the map is constant. Substitute values directly to find images, and set $f(z)=z$ to find fixed points. A Möbius map sends circles and lines to circles or lines, and composing two maps multiplies their matrices. When the question is about zeros, a polynomial of degree $n$ has exactly $n$ zeros in $\mathbb C$, counted with multiplicity, and the roots of $z^n=c$ have modulus $|c|^{1/n}$. By Rouché, if $|g|<|h|$ on $|z|=R$, then $h$ and $h+g$ have equally many zeros inside it.
$$f(z)=\frac{az+b}{cz+d},\quad ad-bc\neq0,\qquad \text{fixed points: }cz^2+(d-a)z-b=0$$

The core intuition here is that a map $\frac{az+b}{cz+d}$ is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero. Fixed points are where the map leaves a point in place, which turns into a quadratic.

*Example:* Find the fixed points of $f(z)=\frac{3z-2}{z}$, where $ad-bc=0+2=2\neq0$.
$$z^2+(0-3)z+2=0\ \Rightarrow\ z=1\text{ or }2$$

*Trap:* Accepting a map with $ad-bc=0$, which is constant, as a Möbius map.

*Check:* Substitute each fixed point into $f$ and confirm $f(z)=z$.

name: First-order ODEs
teach:
When a first-order equation relates $y'$ to $x$ and $y$ and a general or specific solution is asked, identify the form. For a separable equation, divide by $h(y)$, integrate both sides and keep the constant, noting that dividing can lose constant solutions where $h(y)=0$. For a linear equation, multiply through by the factor $\mu$ first. Use the initial value last.
$$y'=g(x)h(y)\Rightarrow\int\frac{dy}{h}=\int g\,dx,\qquad y'+py=q\Rightarrow (\mu y)'=\mu q,\ \mu=e^{\int p}$$

The core intuition here is that the two standard forms can be undone by integration. A separable equation splits into $x$ and $y$ sides, and a linear one becomes an exact derivative after a multiplier.

*Example:* Solve $y'+y=x$ with $y(0)=3$, where $\mu=e^x$.
$$(e^xy)'=xe^x\Rightarrow e^xy=(x-1)e^x+C\Rightarrow y=x-1+4e^{-x}$$

*Trap:* Dropping the exponential in the multiplier, or applying the initial value before the constant is in place.

*Check:* Differentiate the answer. $y'+y=(1-4e^{-x})+(x-1+4e^{-x})=x$.

name: Linear ODEs with constant coefficients
teach:
When a constant-coefficient equation $ay''+by'+cy=0$ is given, solve the characteristic quadratic first. Distinct real roots $r_1,r_2$ give the first form below, and complex roots $\alpha\pm\beta i$ give the second. A repeated root $r$ gives $(c_1+c_2x)e^{rx}$. Then fit $c_1$ and $c_2$ to the starting values, using $y$ and $y'$ at $x=0$. For a constant or polynomial forcing term, try a polynomial of the same degree, times $x$ if it already solves the homogeneous equation.
$$ar^2+br+c=0,\qquad y=c_1e^{r_1x}+c_2e^{r_2x}\ \text{ or }\ e^{\alpha x}(c_1\cos\beta x+c_2\sin\beta x)$$

The core intuition here is that an exponential $e^{rx}$ keeps its shape under differentiation. So it solves the equation exactly when $r$ solves a quadratic, and complex roots give oscillation.

*Example:* Solve $y''+2y'+10y=0$ with $y(0)=2$ and $y'(0)=4$, whose roots are $-1\pm3i$.
$$y=e^{-x}(c_1\cos3x+c_2\sin3x),\qquad c_1=2,\ -c_1+3c_2=4\Rightarrow c_2=2$$

*Trap:* Putting $\beta$ in the exponent where $\alpha$ belongs.

*Check:* The $e^{-x}$ factor means the solution decays, as the negative real part predicts. Also confirm that both starting values hold.

name: ODE systems and phase behavior
teach:
When a system $\mathbf x'=A\mathbf x$ with a $2\times2$ matrix is given and long-run behavior is asked, solve for the eigenvalues, then read the picture. Real with opposite signs gives a saddle. Both negative gives a sink, and both positive gives a source. Purely imaginary gives closed loops. Complex with real part $\alpha\neq0$ gives a spiral, inward if $\alpha<0$.
$$\lambda^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)\lambda+\det A=0$$

The core intuition here is that in an eigenbasis the system splits into scalar equations with solutions $e^{\lambda t}$. The sign of the real part of each eigenvalue says grow or decay.

*Example:* Classify $A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\-2&-1\end{pmatrix}$, where $\operatorname{tr}A=-2$ and $\det A=5$. The real part is negative, so solutions spiral into the origin.
$$\lambda^2+2\lambda+5=0\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda=-1\pm2i$$

*Trap:* Ignoring the sign of the real part, or calling a spiral a saddle.

*Check:* The eigenvalues must sum to the trace.

name: Numerical analysis
teach:
When an integral or a root cannot be found exactly and a formula must approximate it, use the trapezoid rule or Newton's step, where $h=\frac{b-a}{n}$ is the step width. Trapezoid error is of order $h^2$. Simpson's rule uses weights $1,4,2,4,\dots,4,1$ times $\frac h3$ with an even number of intervals, and has error of order $h^4$. Newton's step follows the tangent line to the axis.
$$T=\frac h2\left(f_0+2f_1+\cdots+2f_{n-1}+f_n\right),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k-\frac{f(x_k)}{f'(x_k)}$$

The core intuition here is that each rule replaces the curve by something simple. Higher-order rules cut the error faster as the step shrinks.

*Example:* Estimate $\int_1^3\frac{dx}{x}$ with two intervals, $h=1$.
$$T=\tfrac12\left(1+1+\tfrac13\right)=\tfrac76,\qquad S=\tfrac13\left(1+2+\tfrac13\right)=\tfrac{10}9$$

*Trap:* Using Simpson's rule with an odd number of intervals.

*Check:* The exact value $\ln3\approx1.0986$ lies below both estimates, and Simpson's $1.11$ is closer than the trapezoid's $1.17$.

name: Geometry and transformations
teach:
When a problem asks for a distance to a plane, or for the effect of a rotation, reflection or shear on area, start from the right formula. The distance to the plane $ax+by+cz=d_0$ is given below. For a map, write the images of $e_1$ and $e_2$ as columns. The absolute determinant scales area, and a negative determinant means orientation flips. A triangle with edge vectors $\mathbf u,\mathbf v$ has area $\frac12|\det(\mathbf u\ \mathbf v)|$, and reflection across $y=x$ swaps the coordinates.
$$d=\frac{|ax_0+by_0+cz_0-d_0|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}},\qquad R_\theta=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$$

The core intuition here is that every linear map is fixed by where it sends the unit vectors. Its determinant is the signed factor by which area changes.

*Example:* Find the distance from $(3,1,2)$ to the plane $2x-y+2z=6$.
$$d=\frac{|6-1+4-6|}{\sqrt{4+1+4}}=\frac33=1$$

*Trap:* Leaving out the square root of the normal length, or dropping the absolute value.

*Check:* A point on the plane gives distance $0$.

name: Question triage
teach:
On any timed mixed set where you cannot finish every question at full effort, make a first pass and answer every question you can see through in under a minute. Mark anything that stalls after about thirty seconds, and move on. Return to the marked ones in order of how close you were. Guess before time runs out.
$$\text{time per question}=\frac{\text{total time}}{\text{questions}}$$

The core intuition here is that each question is worth the same, but not each costs the same. Easy points left unread because you sank time into one hard item are lost for nothing.

*Example:* A set has $20$ questions in $50$ minutes, so the budget is $2.5$ minutes each. Suppose the first pass solves $12$ questions in $15$ minutes. That leaves $35$ minutes for the $8$ marked questions, about $4$ minutes each.
$$\frac{50}{20}=2.5\text{ min each},\qquad \frac{50-15}{20-12}=\frac{35}{8}\approx4.4\text{ min each}$$

*Trap:* Spending five minutes on one derivation that a second look later would solve in one.

*Check:* After the first pass, the time left per marked question should exceed the time per question at the start. Here $4.4>2.5$.

name: Plug in the choices
teach:
When a multiple-choice question has a number or formula answer and a long derivation looks likely, start with the simplest numbers or the middle value. Plug each option into the stated equation and discard the ones that fail. If two options survive, test them at a second input.
$$\text{substitute option }x_i\text{ into the condition; keep it only if both sides agree}$$

The core intuition here is that the correct answer is among the options. Testing options often takes less work than solving, and one failed test removes a choice for good.

*Example:* Which $x$ satisfies $2^x+2^{x+1}=24$, from the options $2,3,4,5$? Testing the middle values finds $x=3$ without taking logarithms.
$$x=3:\ 8+16=24\ \checkmark,\qquad x=2:\ 4+8=12\ \times$$

*Trap:* Trusting one test when two options pass it.

*Check:* The chosen option must satisfy every condition in the question, not just the first one you tried.

name: Special-case and symmetry checks
teach:
When options contain a parameter such as $n$, or a matrix or symmetric setup, and the general proof is long, choose $n=1$ or $n=2$, the identity matrix, or a symmetric configuration where the answer is known. Compute the true value there. Then evaluate every option at the same case and cross off those that disagree.
$$\text{true value at a simple case}\ \ne\ \text{option at that case}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{discard}$$

The core intuition here is that a true formula holds in every special case. If an option gives the wrong value in one case, that option is false.

*Example:* The sum $1+2+\cdots+n$ is offered as $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$, $\frac{n^2}{2}$, or $n^2$. At $n=1$ the true value is $1$, which removes the middle option. At $n=2$ the true value is $3$, which removes the last.
$$n=1:\ \frac{1\cdot2}2=1\ \checkmark,\ \ \frac12\ \times,\ \ 1\ \checkmark;\qquad n=2:\ \frac{2\cdot3}{2}=3\ \checkmark,\ \ 2^2=4\ \times$$

*Trap:* Choosing a case so special, like zero, that wrong options also pass.

*Check:* Use two different cases before you commit.

name: Sanity checks
teach:
When you have just derived an answer, or picked one, and a few seconds remain before moving on, ask five questions. Do the units match the quantity asked? Is the sign plausible? Is the size reasonable? Does it behave correctly when a parameter goes to $0$ or grows large? Does it move the right way as an input increases?
$$\text{units, sign, size, limits, and trend of the answer}$$

The core intuition here is that most wrong answers break a basic fact. A quick test of that fact catches slips that a rerun of the algebra repeats.

*Example:* A candidate for the average speed over two legs of equal distance, driven at $30$ and $60$, is $45$. Check the size. The slower leg takes more time, so the average must sit below the midpoint $45$, and the candidate fails.
$$\text{the true value is the harmonic mean }\frac{2\cdot30\cdot60}{30+60}=40$$

*Trap:* Treating a passed check as proof. It only rules out errors.

*Check:* Run at least two of the five tests, in under ten seconds.

name: Time-boxing at pace
teach:
When a test is timed and you are working through it question by question, set a budget per question before you start. At the halfway mark compare the question count with the plan. If you are behind, drop to faster methods and skip sooner. Leave the last minutes for guessing every blank.
$$\text{budget}=\frac{\text{total minutes}}{\text{questions}},\qquad \text{checkpoint at half the time}$$

The core intuition here is that a fixed pace turns drift into a visible number. You notice early when you are behind, while there is still time to adjust.

*Example:* A test has $40$ questions in $100$ minutes. At question $16$ by minute $50$, speed up by skipping anything not started within thirty seconds.
$$\frac{100}{40}=2.5\text{ min},\qquad \text{checkpoint: question }20\text{ by minute }50$$

*Trap:* Spending the last ten minutes on one hard question while easy ones stay blank.

*Check:* The number of questions you have seen should match the clock at each checkpoint.
